items.excerpt: Gholam-Hossein Sa’edi’s The Mourners of Bayal (1964) remains one of the defining works of modern Iranian literature. items.body: Gholam-Hossein Sa’edi’s The Mourners of Bayal (1964) remains one of the defining works of modern Iranian literature. Across eight interconnected stories set in the fictional village of Bayal, Sa’edi explores poverty, famine, superstition, grief and death through a world where collective anxiety gradually erodes the distinction between reality and hallucination. Equally striking is his attention to sound. The village first announces itself acoustically: dogs bark across rooftops, a bell drifts through the darkness, voices pass from window to window, footsteps punctuate long stretches of silence. Bayal is heard before it is fully seen. Tegh & Adel Poursamadi respond directly to this sonic imagination, drawing not on the individual plots of the stories but on their atmosphere and, above all, on the way Sa’edi constructs the village through listening as much as through sight. Like Ima and After You Left, Bayal بیل grew out of extended improvisational dialogues between Tegh’s electronics and Adel Poursamadi’s violin, viola and traditional Iranian instruments before being carefully sculpted into finished compositions. Yet this third collaboration feels markedly more concentrated than its predecessors. The earlier records moved through broader dynamic contrasts, opening onto expansive drones. Bayal بیل occupies a narrower emotional register, maintaining an almost continuous state of subdued tension lending the album a quiet claustrophobia entirely in keeping with Sa’edi’s village, where lives unfold beneath the weight of forces that remain largely unseen. The opening “Black Stone” establishes that landscape from the outset. Electronics and bowed strings emerge from a dense greyscale haze where instrumental identities remain deliberately obscured. Sounds appear like distant outlines. “The Cow” deepens this sense of collective but undefined presence. Throughout the piece, faint layers of indistinct voices drift through the mix like fragments of overheard conversation, suggesting the murmur of Bayal’s unseen inhabitants as they move through alleys and courtyards beyond the listener’s field of perception. These ghostly traces repeatedly dissolve into silence before returning once more, punctuated by resonant strikes that resemble a ritual gong, briefly gathering the surrounding sounds before allowing them to disperse again. The effect closely recalls Sa’edi’s opening pages, where barking dogs, distant bells and whispered exchanges establish the village long before individual characters emerge. “Toward the Vast Mountain” broadens the perspective without abandoning the prevailing sense of enclosure. Percussive markers recur throughout the piece, functioning almost like ritual or processional signals that quietly propel the music forward through its suspended atmosphere. The composition advances with measured inevitability, each percussive gesture subtly reorienting the listener while strings dissolve into electronic residue. “Pāpākh” is the shortest track on the album and refers to the village dog in Sa’edi’s stories, whose barking, pacing and sudden silences are interpreted by Bayal’s deeply superstitious inhabitants as signs of looming disaster. The music mirrors that heightened state of alertness without becoming illustrative. “Zanguleh” occupies a distinctive place within the album. Whereas much of Bayal treats the strings as part of a larger electroacoustic fabric, here Adel Poursamadi’s playing comes decisively to the foreground. Long, lyrical violin lines unfold over a restrained electronic backdrop whose role is less to obscure than to sustain the instrument’s resonance. The piece carries the emotional weight of a lament, offering the album’s clearest expression of grief without disturbing its overall restraint. After the denser first half, its relative transparency feels almost startling. The closing “Under the Willow Tree” follows naturally, letting suspended harmonics, slowly decaying resonance and carefully measured silences carry the emotional weight long after the final sounds have disappeared. The artwork by Atoosa Pourhosseini extends this vision with remarkable coherence. Anonymous figures occupy the margins of a blurred architectural landscape whose contours dissolve beneath mist, grain and diffuse light. The image perfectly reflects Tegh’s description in the liner notes of approaching Sa’edi’s village from the crest of a hill, where movements remain visible but faces, conversations and individual lives disappear into distance. Like the music itself, it withholds detail in favour of atmosphere, inviting the viewer to contemplate Bayal from the same remove that shapes the album’s entire aesthetic. The affinity between Sa’edi’s prose and Tegh and Poursamadi’s music extends beyond mood. The Mourners of Bayal rarely explains events directly, allowing rumour, fragments of dialogue and sensory details to shape the reader’s understanding. Bayal follows the same logic. Voices remain indistinct, instrumental identities blur, and meaning accumulates through resonance, silence and suggestion rather than narrative illustration. Slow, and foreboding, the album faithfully captures the psychological climate of Sa’edi’s fictional village, translating one of the great works of Iranian literature into an electroacoustic language of emotional depth. photo by Aram Tahmasebi To find out more we reached out directly to Tegh and Poursamadi. Unfortuantely, due to the current situation in Iran, only Tegh was available to answer. Ima ایما imagined post-human communication through a dialogue between acoustic instruments, Iranian traditional music and electronics, while After You Left revolved around memory and uncertainty. With Bayal, the starting point is much more concrete: Gholam-Hossein Sa’edi’s The Mourners of Bayal. Yet the new album also feels more restrained and claustrophobic than the previous two, remaining within a remarkably narrow emotional and dynamic range. Did the world of Sa’edi’s book lead you towards this concentration, or was this already a direction your musical dialogue was taking after After You Left? TEGH: Yes, exactly. The atmosphere of the book had a very strong influence on the sound of the album. IMA was supposed to be the first chapter of a larger project. The idea was to continue the project by working with other musicians from different backgrounds and bring different worldviews into the kind of world-building I had in mind. Unfortunately, this part of the project has not really worked out so far. But after the first album, both of us wanted to continue working together. We wanted to keep the colours, contrasts and freedom that we found in the making of IMA, but develop them further and make them more mature. We felt that this could give us a lot of potential for different kinds of experiments, both in terms of meaning and technique. This led to After You Left, and I think it will also be present in some of the work we release in the future. But Bayal follows a different path. I see it as a completely different chapter. As you said, the album stays within the space it presents initially, and to me, the pieces have very simple forms of storytelling, and these qualities came from our personal reading of the atmosphere of the book. In The Mourners of Bayal, it was not so much the events themselves that affected us, but the atmosphere of the book. I feel that this atmosphere does not change very much throughout the book and stays with you. The political and social uncertainty in the stories, the way everything is unreal and yet it becomes believable, and the fact that the stories seem to be made up of people who feel isolated from each other, maybe strangers to one another, and sometimes even strangers to themselves, all affected us. This idea of alienation is present throughout the book. Even in that small fictional village, society itself can hurt and oppress people. The village is surrounded by poverty, death, illness and hunger. All of these things pushed us towards creating a more claustrophobic and oppressive atmosphere in the album. Maybe “post-defeat” is the right word for it. That is my own personal way of describing it. What struck me while reading The Mourners of Bayal is how much of the village Sa’edi constructs through sound: barking dogs, bells, footsteps, voices travelling between houses, and long stretches of silence often precede any clear understanding of what is happening. Your description of approaching Bayal “from the top of a hill”, hearing cries and other sounds without being able to make out their details, seems closely related to this. Were you consciously responding to Sa’edi’s use of sound and listening as literary devices, and how did you translate that sense of hearing a community at a distance into pieces such as “The Cow” and “Pāpākh”? TEGH: I think that is exactly spot on. Sa’edi’s use of sounds, and the way he created the atmosphere of the book through them, was one of the reasons we chose this specific work. It was not really a conscious decision to respond to this aspect of the book. We never really sat down and talked about choosing this direction. I think we were simply influenced by it to such an extent that it found its way into the album naturally. For example, there is the sound of the bell attached to the empty carriage, coming from far away in the desert. It is mentioned several times throughout the book, often in connection with moments where there is death. The character of this sound, and the meaning it carries, had a strong effect on us and led us towards making “Zanguleh,” which means “bell” in Farsi. It might sound strange or unrelated, but this carriage and its bell also remind me of the cart in Béla Tarr’s The Turin Horse. It creates a very heavy image like that in my mind. The idea of looking at the events from a distance, as if we were standing on top of a hill looking at the village, came from our wish not to create a direct sonic retelling of the book. This perspective allowed us to stay away from simply recreating the events and focus more on what we personally felt from the atmosphere of the book and do our own thing based on that. We wanted to make music based on the effect the book had on both of us, rather than trying to represent the story itself. That is also why we left quite a lot of time between reading the book and starting to make the music. We wanted to forget as many details of the stories as possible and work only with what had remained in our minds, and of course it helped us avoid using the sounds from the book in a more literal way. For example, Papākh, the village dog, is one of the most important characters in the book for me. He has a strong presence, and in a way he observes everything while remaining silent and the villagers have a strange relationship with him. In general, the villagers have very close relationships with animals. The relationship between Mashdi Hassan and his cow, Islam and his goat, Papākh and the villagers, all stayed in my mind. The fact that this is a village suffering from famine, where some people have to go from one village to another to beg or steal food, but they still do not kill their animals for food, was particularly striking to me. The two tracks came out of this. We were more interested in making music out of the feeling we got from the presence of these characters in the story, rather than directly referring to the sound of Papākh or Mashdi Hassan’s cow. You describe the recording process as a series of improvisational dialogues that were subsequently processed and structured, with responding to the concept taking precedence over conventional musical rules. From your perspective, how does that process work? When Adel produces a sound, are you responding to it electronically in real time, or do the more radical transformations happen later during editing and processing? And at what point, for you, does an improvisation cease to be the documentation of a performance and become a composed piece? TEGH: Naturally, this way of working was not something new for Adel and me. We worked in an almost similar way on the two previous albums as well. We talked a lot about the effect the atmosphere of the book had on us. We both knew what elements of it made us hear things, and what kind of feelings we wanted to communicate. But we never really talked about what the tracks should sound like, what their structure should be, or what we should or should not do. The process usually started with one of us doing something, and the other responding to it. This would continue through different sessions, and then we would listen back to the recordings. Sometimes, from a one-hour recording, only one melody and one beat would come out, like in “Toward the Vast Mountain.” We felt that they were close to the concept we had in mind, and then we developed them into a track at a later stage. “Zanguleh” and “The Black Stone,” for example, both came out of the recording of a single session. A lot of the changes and processing happened afterwards, especially the processing of the sounds and shaping the forms. This was important for bringing the different sounds together and making them feel like they belonged to the same world. One of the main reasons for this is that I am honestly not a very good improviser. In many of the sessions, instead of being able to immediately reach the sound I had in mind, I was more often just leaving some kind of indication of what I wanted to reach later. For example going back to “Toward the Vast Mountain,” I had already written a beat for the melody in the improvisation, but the sounds and the pattern were quite different from what you hear on the final track. As for the last part of your question, it is a little difficult to explain. There is a point during the process when you suddenly think, “Ah, we found it. This is becoming something.” It is a moment when you find each other, everything starts to work together, and you feel that you have reached something. For me, that is the point where I can change the way I look at the material. I can stop thinking only about finding sounds or making the improvisation work, and start looking at what we have from the perspective of storytelling and how the idea can develop, where it can go, and how it can become a composition. artwork by Atoosa Pour Hosseini One of the most affecting moments for me is “Zanguleh”, because Adel’s violin suddenly becomes much more exposed and lyrical after spending much of the record partially submerged within the electroacoustic texture; it almost functions as a lament before “Under the Willow Tree” carries the record towards silence. Across Ima ایما , After You Left and now Bayal بیل, has your understanding of the relationship between strings and electronics changed? Are you increasingly interested in making it difficult to tell where one ends and the other begins, and what made you choose to break that ambiguity so strikingly on “Zanguleh”? TEGH: Absolutely. One of the things I personally question now after several years of working with Adel is exactly this. In IMA, and to some extent in After You Left, there is still quite a clear distance between the sound of the instruments and the electronics. Maybe you could say that the meeting between my world and Adel’s world did not always become a third world, something that was neither completely mine nor completely his. I think this improved in After You Left, and we got even closer to it with Bayal. I would not necessarily say that I am trying to make it difficult to tell the sounds apart. What is more important to me is that, in the composition, sound design and all the different stages of the process, I do not treat the instruments and electronics as separate things. I also try not to let the source of a sound decide how I treat it. I want to reach a point where by the end of the process there is a kind of continuity between the sounds, and they feel like they belong to the same family. It does not matter whether you can recognise where each sound comes from, what matters is that when these different sonic characters are put together, they do not feel like they have been taken from completely different worlds and simply placed next to each other like a collage. As for “Zanguleh,” as I mentioned earlier, the track was influenced by the sound of the bell coming from far away in the story. In my personal interpretation, I connect this sound with death, not as an ending, but as something that has been staying with you. As you said, that section was meant to work almost like a lament. It is actually a mourning. Our idea was for the track to reach a point where it could finally break out and mourn freely, and that is where the track ended up. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Tegh与Adel Poursamadi的第三次合作，灵感源自伊朗现代文学经典《Bayal哀悼者》。两人以电子设备与小提琴、中提琴及伊朗传统乐器进行长时段即兴对话，再雕琢成完整作品。与前作相比，此作动态范围更窄，持续维持一种低沉的紧张感，营造出与原作小说中村庄封闭氛围相呼应的听觉体验。开场曲《Black Stone》以电子音与拉弦乐器从灰暗的混响中浮现，乐器身份模糊不清；《The Cow》中飘忽不定的人声碎片暗示村庄中隐形居民的喃喃低语，被仪式般的钟声打断后又归于沉寂；《Toward the Vast Mountain》则以节拍标记推进，节奏缓慢而不可逆转。整张专辑将伊朗文学的声学想象转化为声音作品，模糊了现实与幻觉的边界，是实验电子与传统器乐融合的典范。

items.body: Shell and Core takes its title from the unfinished concrete structures that have become fixtures of the Syrian landscape, and Tasgeelat Al-Husni تسجيلات الحُسني uses that image of arrested construction as a way of looking at lives left incomplete. Much of the record is assembled from things heard or observed in everyday life: bureaucratic rituals, checkpoints, cars, street conversations, scrap collectors and an uncle’s absurd political opinions. On “Spacetune” these details accumulate into a comic story that deliberately goes nowhere; “Existing” turns repetition and waiting into its subject, while the heavier “Grinder” pushes familiar material towards something more grotesque. The humour is important. Rather than presenting Syria exclusively through catastrophe, Tasgeelat Al-Husni draws on a local tradition of satire and everyday mockery in which absurdity is one means of living with circumstances that have themselves become absurd. The music operates in much the same way, refusing a clean division between local tradition and experimental electronics. The oud can introduce the relatively spacious “Existing”, sit behind electronic and guitar noise on “Spacetune”, or grind against doom-laden riffs on “Grinder”. Al-Husni explicitly rejects using the instrument as a nostalgic signifier of a disappearing culture; here it belongs to the present as naturally as synthesis, distortion or field recording. Progressive and heavy rock are equally embedded in the record’s vocabulary, particularly in its abrupt shifts between calm and physical weight. Lazar Mečanin’s production makes those contrasts unusually pronounced: passages of relative openness can suddenly thicken into distortion, low-frequency pressure and noise, giving the album the unstable logic of the environment it describes. One of the album’s most striking changes of register comes on “Perspective”, where the voice of Ukrainian opera singer Oksana Vakula introduces a radiant tone, briefly opening up the record’s otherwise rough and unstable sonic terrain. That makes the unfinished Massar Discovery Center on the cover more than an illustration. Along with Syria’s other abandoned concrete shells, it becomes an architectural counterpart to a record about interrupted trajectories. Yet Shell and Core avoids turning incompletion into a grand metaphor. What matters most is the peripheral and the discarded: things overheard, jokes, irritating routines, incongruous sounds and surreal encounters. The picture of Syria that emerges is at the same time damaged and precarious, but also mundane and funny, a place whose exposed structural bones are filled with everyday life. To help us better understand the production process for Shell and Core we reached out directly to Tasgeelat Al-Husni. Throughout عَ العَضم (Shell and Core), everyday Syrian life is depicted in a way that often feels almost surreal, allowing the ordinary and the mythical to coexist. The repeated “unknown” in “Spacetune”, the taxi driver nicknamed Azrael—the Angel of Death—blasting heavy dabke, the endless bureaucracy of “Existing”, the Ladas, and finally the litany of scrap collectors all feel like fragments of the same social landscape. There is also a distinctly sardonic humour running through the writing. Do you think of your lyrics as poetry, documentary montage, social commentary or simply another way of composing with sound? Most of the lyrics are rephrasing of something I have heard in Syria either in a conversation with friends or randomly on the street. I wrote down some of what I had heard and then integrated them with how I thought of each song. I am new to writing words, so I don’t know much, but I have tried writing a comical story with mild suspense that leads nowhere on “Spacetune,” describing recurrent scenes from daily life on “Existing,” and creating some surreal visual scenes on “Grinder.” The sardonic humor is essential to the environment where the album came from. It’s in the music we hear (such as the music of the Rahbani family), the TV we watch (such as Spotlight – بقعة ضوء), the books we read (such as Muhammad al-Maghut’s), so you would also hear it in your day-to-day life from your relatives, your college friends, the bus driver or even from a soldier on a checkpoint. Add to that the absurdity of people’s takes on the conflict, like that uncle on Spacetune, which naturally calls for mockery. Peugeot 504 – photo by Hussain Hussain The second track, “Existing”, opens with an oud before gradually expanding into a much broader electronic landscape. The instrument never feels nostalgic or symbolic of tradition; instead, it becomes another texture within the composition. Was it important for you to avoid treating the oud as a marker of cultural identity, allowing it instead to coexist naturally with electronics and noise? It was! I think such instruments are not supposed to sound like a distant cry from the past echoing in an empty space, or “a ghostly remnant from a lost culture”, like David Byrne once wrote. The oud, like any instrument, should be used to serve the song the way the song is meant to be. It definitely could be used in its classical character with takasim and as accompaniment for singing like on “Existing,” but it can also accompany heavy doom metal riffs to add a bloody drilling texture on “Grinder,” or do some finger picking behind synth and guitar noises like on Spacetune. If you listen to a based folk performance from the past, you hear the oud vital and integrated with the rest of the instruments, not sounding like an anomaly, and I think this is how it should be treated in any other (modern) context. Window – photo by Hussain Hussain Although the album is rooted in electroacoustic composition and experimental electronics, there are moments—particularly in the treatment of distortion, low-frequency weight and rhythmic pressure—that recall progressive rock, heavy rock and noise. Are those traditions part of your musical vocabulary, and how do they intersect with the experimental and electronic music you make today? These traditions strongly influence how we have approached this record and music making in general. The treatment of sound at this level was more Lazar’s part, so I have forwarded the question to him, and this is his response: “Those traditions have to be a part of our vocabulary given the fact it’s the music we grew up on – Floyd, Crimson, etc. These bands influenced us as players but they also influenced how we think about music. A song can exhibit cinematic properties and sometimes be even more immersive than a movie if done right. The record is really a landscape representing every-day life in Syria (if I understood it correctly myself hah), moments of beauty and calmness intertwined with unpredictable chaos mostly right next to each other, so in a way the music is interpreting life, and by using these acoustic and production techniques we are attempting to recreate the feelings one might have simply living there.” Random Structure – photo by Hussain Hussain How do you see your work in relation to other Syrian experimental musicians? Is there a shared aesthetic or set of concerns emerging from the scene, or do you feel that each artist is responding to the experiences of recent years in fundamentally different ways? I have learned a lot from contemporary Syrian and Arab artists — Tootard, Shabjdeed, Khaled Allaf, Lynn Adib, Al-Rahel Al-Kabir, Kulna Sawa, and many more — and that has encouraged me to work on my own stuff, sing about what I have heard or seen, and eventually release that. It is true that everyone is responding to their experiences in their own way; some express that in a desperate way, some in a cynical way, some tackle social issues, and some speak about personal experiences. Maybe what we have in common is our frustration and disgust with our situation now and in recent years, but who knows? What’s important to me is that many of our artists sound so fresh, so unique and so relevant, and I always look forward to hearing their new approaches and what they are talking about. The cover features the unfinished Massar Discovery Center (“Massar Rose”) in Damascus—a project that was meant to embody education, innovation and the future before construction stopped in 2014. Throughout the album, there is a recurring sense of lives shaped by interruption: bureaucratic waiting, checkpoints, abandoned trajectories and systems that never quite reach completion. Did you see the building as encapsulating that condition, or were you drawn to it for different reasons? Gardenia Towers – photo by Hussain Hussain Exactly, hence the name, ع العضم Shell and Core! The rest of the album art (partly prepared for a CD release) features some well-known incomplete buildings, such as the infamous 50-year-old Yalbugha Tower in the middle of the capital and the Gardenia Towers in Homs that became known among the public as the “Death Towers”, used by snipers during the war. Such giant incomplete, mostly ugly, structures are so common to see in Syria. They are ironically reflective of the life of Syrian individual that has become so crippled, it might never reach a sense of completion. Everyone who lost their home forever and had to live in a tent, everyone that lost their beloved ones, got detained for the stupidest reason, or had to serve in the army for 8 years or so, and also everyone who just had to live or grow up there during these awful times. To me, this building not only encapsulates these incomplete trajectories, but also resembles, with its bare bones (عضم) sticking out, how naked, exposed and fragile we are. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: 叙利亚音乐人Tasgeelat Al-Husni以未完工建筑为隐喻，将日常声音碎片——官僚仪式、检查站、街头对话、废品回收者——拼贴进电子与厂配实验的肌理中。奥德琴不再被当作消失文化的怀旧符号，而是与合成器、失真、场域录音并置在当下。Lazar Mečanin的制作刻意放大平静与重压之间的突兀切换，营造出与环境本身一样不稳定的听觉逻辑。乌克兰歌剧歌手Oksana Vakula在Perspective中的声线短暂打开粗糙音景，带来罕见的明亮质感。专辑拒绝将叙利亚简化为灾难叙事，而是从地方讽刺传统出发，让荒诞与日常共存，在未竟的轨迹中描绘出一个既破损又充满人间烟火的生活图景。

items.body: This new release from the Belgian act Hybryds is a remarkable record. The title leaves little to the imagination, focusing—as the work of many artists across various disciplines has so often done—on the seven deadly sins. What makes this release particularly intriguing, however, is that four of the tracks date back to 2002, originally appearing on the “Lust”-EP released by Spectre. After all these years, the original singer, Miss Poly-Ester, got back in touch with Sandy Nijs and asked him to complete the album. So Sandy returned to the music, and the lost tracks were finally completed with the singer’s vocals. In total, we are treated to eleven tracks. Alongside the songs addressing the seven deadly sins, there are extras such as an intro and two live tracks dating from 2003. Hybryds has continued to surprise me in recent years. The project remains true to its trademark Ritualistic style, yet everything sounds more modern. This record stands out in particular for its slow, infectious, Trip-Hop-like rhythms. At times, I get the impression of hearing an Industrial version of Tricky—and that is very much intended as a huge compliment. After all, Hybryds naturally retains that familiar industrial DNA. The atmosphere remains dark, mysterious, and unsettling, evoking the feeling of stepping into a forbidden place where a certain decadence gradually sweeps you away. This impression is further reinforced by the artistic and highly explicit booklet accompanying the album, allowing Sandy Nijs to indulge his interest in and inspiration from fetish culture through a series of photographs that remain closely connected to the central theme. It is the kind of booklet that algorithms would rapidly detect and block instantly. Fortunately, there are still artists daring enough to go there—artists for whom it isn’t simply about nudity, provocation, or shock value. The music is far too good for that. I wouldn’t claim that Hybryds have reinvented themselves, but in recent years they have clearly been riding a new wave of inspiration, and this record is a fine example of where that has taken them. The older live tracks don’t exactly add much value, but the rest of the album is simply magnificent. As far as I’m concerned, it’s one of the best albums I’ve discovered this year. It would be a true sin to let this particular gem pass you by… (Ratring:9). Listen to “Envy”: Envy by Hybryds About Hybryds Hybryds is a Belgian project centered on Sandy Nys, active since the mid-1980s and known for ritual, mythical and industrial electronic work rooted in the cassette-era Belgian underground. Nys’ career began with the 1986 cassette “Mythical Music From The 21st Century,” followed by releases including “Music For Rituals” (1992) and “The Ritual Of The Rave” (1995). In the 1990s Hybryds became a duo with Leen Smets (Yasnaïa); from 2000 Nys continued the project solo before German vocalist Madeline joined, with multi-instrumentalist Peter De Koning later expanding the lineup. On 3RioArt / Zoharum, Hybryds has released “Mythopia” (2022), “Mythopia, The Sequel” (2024), “In The Wake Of The Witch” (2025), “Fire And Ice, Flesh And Bones Part 1 & 2” (2026) and “Desert Of White Salt” (2026). “7even Deadly Sins” follows on the same labels, reworking four tracks that originally appeared on the 2002 “Lust” EP on Spectre with new vocals by Madeline and Katherina.
items._cn_summary: 比利时老牌工业计划Hybryds以七宗罪为概念回归，四首来自2002年的旧作经主唱Miss Poly-Ester重新合作后补全，搭配全新曲目与两首2003年现场录音共十一首。专辑延续了项目标志性的仪式感氛围，暗黑、神秘、令人不安，同时融入缓慢而具有感染力的Trip-Hop式节奏，听感上接近工业化的Tricky。工业DNA贯穿始终，但整体音色比以往更为现代。配套画册以恋物文化摄影呼应主题，视觉与音乐共同构建堕落的仪式空间。作为地下独立厂牌发行的作品，保留了算法时代罕见的艺术勇气，而非仅靠裸露制造冲击。

items.body:
This column is a loose gathering of recordings – two duos, two quartets – that might define a certain frontier, a degree of meaning in improvised interactivity spreading over 12 years. At times, the combination of close listening and simultaneous writing (the only way I can find to describe this music) results in verbal collisions that may be elusive in meaning, but they may also legitimately represent some of the transformative complexity and overlapping visions arising in these works of essentially collective invention. Though one of these recordings is more than a decade old, they may represent a kind of perpetual edge.

Certain musics can pass through walls of custom, identity, and meaning, assuming unknown shapes, escaping any strict verbal denotation, meaning becoming at once plastic and ineffable. Such music cannot be analyzed or described successfully, such failed exercises, however, perhaps contributing to both its mystery and its beauty, music that might suggest a hymn from an unknown culture, possibly disappeared, to an unknown deity, possibly deceased. In collectively improvised music, the role of the listener is paramount: assembling, collecting, composing ... At the same time, however, no interpretation is more privileged than another. These particular recordings are by musicians who can create dreams in sound. Some will imagine mills or factory floors, tuned to and amplifying unimaginable inventions of human industry. Empathy contributes a mutating, transformational soundscape. These are musics that create uncommon space.

Die Dritte Ebene (45 rpm LP, NiVuNiConnu, nvnc-lp062) by Emilio Gordoa and the late Sven-Åke Johansson might initially seem exotic. Ultimately, it’s not. It’s work of perfect transparency, that is, a view of whatever one hears as the other side of anywhere. The cover offers two titles, DIE DRITTE EBEN or EL TERCER NIVEL, “the third level,” in German or Spanish, with each phrase written with the “E”s written as reversed 3s. The phrase arises in Gordoa’s brief description appended to the Bandcamp page: “We were discussing how our music moves as if in parallel lines, and how after a while something third will emerge from it, almost like a ghost. It is something I find almost mystical: how this third level manifested itself in our playing without us thinking about it.”

Reminiscent of Johansson’s previous NiVuNiConnu release, Tea Time, with Nicholas Bussmann and Yan Jun, the music hints at Erik Satie’s Furniture Music, somehow constituting a radical background music that enhances consciousness, the special resonance of repeated materials creating a trance-like, near-ecstatic state, a reflective consciousness that rises between the parts created by Johansson and Gordoa, illuminating as well as hypnotic. Die Dritte Ebene, from August 26, 2023, points to an ineffable quality – a kind of trance, a kind of lift, a spectral point of attention that is produced in a listener’s collaboration with the close echoes, tight resonance and metallic rattle of Johansson’s snare, the reeds of his accordion, and the glassy ring of Gordoa’s vibraphone, glowing like light in sonic form. The shared insistence and simultaneity of Johansson and Gordoa’s work consistently expands what is essentially a minimalist musical environment, concluding with a strange abstraction of accordion and vibraphone that might suggest a kind of musical haunting.

Nate Wooley and Seymour Wright recorded About Trumpet and Saxophone in 2012, appearing on the Fataka label in 2013. While that release was unquestionably radical, its forthcoming successor, recorded in 2025, About Saxophone and Trumpet (Relative Pitch) takes a very different initial tack, opening with a deconstruction of the romantic ballad “The Midnight Sun,” composed by Lionel Hampton and Sonny Burke in 1947, recorded initially as an instrumental, with sufficient melodic grace to have lyrics later added by Johnny Mercer, spurring recordings by June Christy, Ella Fitzgerald, and Carmen McRae. Here the melody is clearly audible through a series of gasps, honks, and shattered, incomplete phrases, a nod to tradition that rapidly expands, becoming increasingly inclusive.

There follows “Experiment Four,” an extended dialogue which includes some of the strangest sounds ever emitted by saxophone and trumpet, often coming from very different positions in the sound spectrum. The fourth track, “Untitled,” is genuinely conversational, though the conversation is conducted in assorted bleats and blasts. Each musician is repeatedly triggered by the other’s material, whether pinching their sound inward, or adapting a radical extroversion. Music here will stand in for complex human relationships and perceptions, a sound store evolving to mark the impact of events in one’s daily life, worlds for which artists have long been refining their techniques and perceptions. As our descriptive apparatus daily fails before global events, our key artists stretch the elements. In that sense, call it modern syntactical practice or a soundtrack to Guernica, but the expressive range in which Wooley and Wright here operate seems perfectly in keeping with the daily news. Meanwhile, the inner tunings and sustained tones, even their matching fast vibratos suggest the development and synergy of an expressionist language. Sudden shifts will swiftly resemble elegant balladry of yore, echoes of that “Midnight Sun.”

While the Wooley/Wright duet recalls Fataka, Trevor Brent’s remarkable label – “‘dedicated to releasing recordings of small group and solo improvisations with a particular interest in situations where a common musical language has not yet fully emerged” – has become active again, releasing Parallels & Diagonals by a quartet from the label’s earlier period, 14th July 2014 at Cafe Oto, in which Wooley and Wright appear in a quartet with two percussionists active since the dawn of English free improvisation, Paul Lytton and Eddie Prévost. Contrary to Brent’s explanation of the label (and a genuine generational difference: the percussionists had discographies before the wind players were born), the four musicians seem so closely attuned – each a genuine spontaneous composer – that they sound like they might have had a long history together. Parallels and Diagonals is 12-year-old music, but it sounds like it might be recorded next year.

The opening track, the extended Parallel A, sounds like a machine shop that has discovered free improvisation, shifting dramatically after a passage of silence shortly after the 15-minute mark. The sounds suggest a light roll on a kettle drum, a brush on a cymbal, the sound of air pushed delicately through a trumpet. This notion of interiority marks the collective passage of these musicians, finding a terrain at once both barely imagined and yet a defining part of the human condition. In Diagonal A, fundamental gestures, like air squeezed through a metal tube, take on their own significance, behaving like Buddhist mudras, invoking fundamental gestures and symptoms of human life, murmurs, signs, abrasions. Diagonal B’s rapid actions and continuous overlapping suggest activity so closely attended by the musicians that it might follow a score in which the pauses might be carefully accounted, floating among a delicately bowed cymbal, other sounds that cannot be identified, and some that shimmer around audibility.

foam and mesh (Fundacja Słuchaj Records) by the B:A:N:S BAND is the work of pianist Sophie Agnel, saxophonist John Butcher, bassist Pascal Niggenkemper, and percussionist Ståle Liavik Solberg, recorded at the 2024 ArtAct Festival in St. Johann, Austria. While it’s the only grouping here with a conventional instrumental grouping, the orientation of the musicians will ensure that there is nothing resembling convention in the ways that the instruments are utilized.

foam and mesh I is clearly the main event, a 35-minute dialogue in which four of the most skilled spontaneous composers put together a dense weave of sonic events, with nothing predictable, yet everything interlocking. Tension curves are developed with astonishing power, each member of the quartet seemingly pursuing a unique and independent path, yet everything contributing to an astonishing rhythmic taffy-pull in which every part contribute to a compound and original overall momentum. This complex relationship will sustain through numerous group movements, whether slow balladic ruminations with isolated knocks and flurries or a sudden tense wedding of trembling oscillations, all four musicians regularly finding distinct timbres. The relatively brief foam and mesh II initially foregrounds Agnel’s piano, her focus initially on brief, isolated, tight-knit clusters with abstract flurries from Niggenkemper’s bass and the randomizing knitwork of Liavik Solberg. When Butcher initially enters on soprano saxophone, the random patterns generally coalesce into a continuous stream of different rhythms and complementary densities before the work’s ultimately gradual disappearance.
items._cn_summary: 这是一篇聚焦集体即兴创作的乐评，涵盖两组二重奏与两组四重奏的录音横跨十二年的探索。评论强调演奏者之间通过密切聆听与同步书写式的互动，形成可塑而难以言说的音乐形态。Gordoa与Johansson的二重奏专辑呈现透明质感，声音在平行线中交汇出某种第三层面的幽灵般浮现，呼应Satie式家具音乐的理念，将重复材料发展为近似出神冥想的共振空间。整体音乐超越了习俗与身份的边界，在听者的参与下不断重构，强调共情与声音景观的变形力量。评论以诗化语言探讨即兴音乐中聆听者的核心角色，指出这种音乐既无法被分析也不应被单一诠释所限定。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是内罗毕新厂牌Cool Waters的首发作品，由德国出生、肯尼亚定居的打击乐手Sven Kacirek与Olith Ratengo组成的二人组Odd Okoddo，邀请83岁的肯尼亚东部传统歌手Ogoya Nengo共同录制。音乐以Kacirek的Buchla合成器、手打打击乐和偶尔的架子鼓为核心，与两位歌手的人声交织。歌曲从简朴的节奏敲击起步，逐渐叠加4/4拍律动、低音线和木琴般的音色层，最终合成多声部复合节奏，与人声浑然一体。乐评将这类跨文化合作归入"folktronica"范畴，与Chouk Bwa及Nyege Nyege厂牌的探索性作品同列，强调当代非洲音乐在保持深厚传统根基的同时，通过电子手段实现前卫化的能力。白人电子音乐家与高龄传统歌手的组合，本身就是文化交融的缩影。

items.album: John Coltrane 100: John Coltrane in Detroit, June 1966
items.excerpt: John Coltrane Memorial in Hamlet, N.C. Photographer unknown. By Stuart Broomer If I can write anything meaningful about the music of John Coltrane, it may be about the context in which I came to experience his work live, in 1966, after listening intently to his work for four years on record and writing reviews of some of it as well. One’s juvenilia is embarrassing almost by definition, but that’s my particular gateway here to a world in which Coltrane was playing live a few feet in front of me.
items.body: John Coltrane Memorial in Hamlet, N.C. Photographer unknown. By Stuart Broomer If I can write anything meaningful about the music of John Coltrane, it may be about the context in which I came to experience his work live, in 1966, after listening intently to his work for four years on record and writing reviews of some of it as well. One’s juvenilia is embarrassing almost by definition, but that’s my particular gateway here to a world in which Coltrane was playing live a few feet in front of me. 13 months later he passed away. I write this hopefully to communicate something of the challenging world in which Coltrane made his music, that ever more intense, more radically free music, as testimony to his courage and vision as a great artist, as large a person as one might be in that world. The John Coltrane Reference (Routledge, 2008) by Chris DeVito, Yasuhiro Fujioka, Wolf Schmaler and David Wild, edited by Lewis Porter (Routledge, 2008) is a monumental work of scholarship. After the introductions, there’s a Chronology of Coltrane’s life and career that runs to 357 large pages of fine print, followed by a Discography of 404 similarly sized pages in identical print, followed by 49 more pages of appendices, index, etc. Very near the Chronology’s conclusion, there’s an entry for the John Coltrane Quintet’s appearance at Detroit’s Drome Lounge from June 17-26, 1966. The personnel, then consistent, is identified as Coltrane, tenor and soprano saxophones; Pharoah Sanders, tenor saxophone; Alice Coltrane, piano; Jimmy Garrison, bass; Rasheid Ali, drums, Friday to Sunday, matinees on Sunday. Reviewed in Coda (“John Coltrane Quintet – Drome Bar—Detroit” by Stu Broomer, Aug-Sept., 1966, pp.32 - 33). The review is represented by just a few of its sentences, but I’ll restrict myself to the Reference editor’s choices and their punctuation as well. “This is probably the most moving working band in America (…) Tenor saxophonist Farrell “Pharoah” Sanders is now the most important soloist in the group. (…) When (Coltrane) first heard Albert Ayler in 1962, Coltrane told him he had heard himself playing like that in a dream once. (…). This band has recorded five times but nothing has been released. Perhaps Bob Thiele is hoping Coltrane will return to his old-time sanity. I for one hope he will not”. (Reprinted by permission of the author. All Rights Reserved). What I’m trying to get at here about John Coltrane is an essential drive for expression and liberation, for liberation from every constraint to discover what’s real or what’s at least possible. If my memories from 60 years ago mean anything, they’re about the value of revolt and the horror of the norm, the judgmental restriction of cultural norms, in some places becoming more restrictive than anything I might have felt 60 years ago (a festival of liberalism by comparison). As a result, I want the music more intense, more personal, more unpredictable and I’ll stand up for it anywhere. But it is not without ambiguities. As a teenager in the 1960s, I became obsessed with free jazz. It was a promise of freedom from restraint as well as constraint, an explosion of mixed emotions from great sorrow to ecstasy, in effect, perhaps, a promise too far. My absorption in jazz had begun in childhood with the 1957 TV special The Sound of Jazz and followed with the eventual LP. More television: I saw the Robert Herridge Presents episode with Miles Davis and John Coltrane in 1960 and loved it. My brief initial puzzlement and rapid-onset rapture with free jazz started when I picked up the September 1961 Metronome at the corner variety store. It included an epic essay on the jazz avantgarde by the then LeRoi Jones (I still have the essay somewhere — stapled together — the issue is gone). The writing was abstract, mannered and strange but also enchanting (I had already read a paperback of Kerouac’s Tristessa ), its subject an arcane revolution. By the time I had purchased Ornette! and Free Jazz a few months later, Metronome had ceased to exist. I had only Down Beat , a magazine at the time sufficiently reactionary to condemn John Coltrane and Eric Dolphy as anti-jazz in a cover story. A few years later, circa 1965, I started writing for Coda, then Canada’s only jazz magazine. If there’s a shock in that original account (in bowdlerized form), it’s likely the ranking of Sanders’ performance over Coltrane’s. Without digging for the original, I recall moments from that night when I was listening to the dense, tumultuous music and focussing on the brilliant screaming mayhem of the two saxophones, only to open my eyes and discover that John Coltrane was intently hitting a cowbell with a drumstick and Pharoah Sanders was the only person playing a saxophone. This isn’t a criticism of Coltrane. He was one of the greatest musicians who ever played jazz, but we all know now that he was seriously ill and still carrying a heavy musical load. Other memories: I already had certain knowledge that Jimmy Garrison’s solos, as memorably powerful as they were, depended heavily on the bass’s tuning in fourths, and the complex, droning solos dependent to a significant degree on the use of open strings (I was a bass player at the time). At one point in the evening, Coltrane spoke quietly to him (I was sitting at a piano-shaped stage, my ear within four feet of their mouths) specifying the key for one of his extended introductions. Garrison then looked upset, arguing for another key. I wasn’t surprised by the issue. I was surprised that it was happening about four years into Garrison’s tenure in the band. Another and crucial surprise goes to the heart of the history of free jazz. My party (myself and three others, young musicians from Toronto, three Caucasian, one Japanese) were, in effect, insiders (however “out” we might feel in the Drome). We arrived early, conveying Rashied to the venue since we were staying in the same place, the Detroit Artists Workshop. Arriving early, we found a strange mix of conviviality and formality. Standing just inside the foyer, Jimmy Garrison was shaking hands with patrons as they entered. Even to a bass player, Garrison’s right hand (the plucking one) came as a shock: it felt like a bundle of sticks. As popular, as great , as John Coltrane was, there was a fundamental divide in the audience about the shape his music was assuming, that was apparent from the time the music began (a shock perhaps influenced by the very music that Impulse was choosing to release). In essence there were two audiences. In the Drome it happened largely along racial lines, generally slightly older blacks on the one hand, and the white audience, many significantly younger, significantly suspended between hip and hippie. One audience looked disgruntled, offering spare, obligatory applause; the other clapped wildly with exclamatory shouts. Late in the evening, Coltrane broke into the opening phrase of his anthem, “My Favorite Things”, its bright coiling phrases instantly recognizable from the first note. It was amazing. With my back to the rest of the audience, I could actually feel the room lift, so strong was the shift in mood, comparable, for a brief instant, to the sun breaching a cloud cover. Within a couple of minutes, the sonic tumult had taken over again, and one could feel, even more intensely, the mood of the room dropping, to frustration and disappointment, perhaps, and most intensely, I felt, the abandonment, the sense of betrayal. In total, (expanding on Coltrane's grimly disappointed Black audience) the trip seemed at times to be about race but things would get much darker, or should I say lighter (toxic metaphors lurk in our tongue) -- I had gone there with three other young Toronto musicians with whom I played. I had an association with John Sinclair (then in jail on drug charges -- not sure how current John's name is, but his greatest moment of celebrity came when imprisoned during Woodstock: Abby Hoffman interrupted the beginning of the Who's performance with a comment to the effect that Woodstock didn't mean shit while John Sinclair was in jail; then Pete Townsend hit Hoffman with his guitar for trying to take over the Who's stage). In John’s absence, his partner Leni Sinclair was running the Workshop. I knew The Detroit Artists Workshop through shared performances between Detroit and Toronto, performances arranged by John Sinclair and the Toronto poet Victor Coleman of the Bohemian Embassy, a Toronto coffee house and performance space. Shared performances had included members of Detroit trumpeter Charles Moore’s MC5 with featured musicians that had included Marion Brown and Andrew Hill (through which I got to play bass with Andrew for a weekend among other playing associations). I had also published a poem and a record review in John's mimeo'd music journal Changes , which I think may have only gone to two (or maybe three) issues. The Workshop was the epicentre of radical culture in Detroit whether the issue was music, race, drugs, economics or language. Later it was the spawning ground of the MC5, of "Up Against the Wall Motherfucker" fame, who John Sinclair managed. He later was a founder of the White Panther Party, a Black Panther support group. When I met the members of [Ahmed] a few years ago in Guelph, talk turned to Detroit. Some members were thinking about visiting Detroit, and Pat Thomas and I found ourselves reminiscing about John, whose poetry Pat had accompanied during an Amsterdam performance. John's contract, Pat recalled, required a private pot smoking loft. A few days before our group arrived in Detroit, a young inter-racial couple from the Workshop had been violently attacked on the street by the sons of a former Mississippi sheriff whose property adjoined the Workshop at the rear. While we were staying there, the sheriff had invited the residents of the Workshop to a get together/ barbecue to make peace. None of the Workshop residents (naturally) wanted to go and Leni Sinclair asked our Toronto group (whom they were temporarily housing, four males sufficiently groomed to get across the border without close scrutiny) to go as their representatives. We accepted with a certain reluctance, though things (barbecue, blanched pleasantries) went civilly enough. An hour later, on the way out of Detroit, we stopped at an ice cream outlet before we hit the border. The sons and their wives and children were there as well. On neutral ground, none of us acknowledged the existence of the other. Charles Tyler, Stuart Broomer + Perry Robinson, 1966 ©2014 Bill Copeland AN AFTERWORD: 60 years on, I frequently listen to John Coltrane recordings, probably more than to any other historical jazz artist. I have the complete runs of the Prestige and Atlantic recordings and most of the Impulses on CD and the recordings with Monk and Miles Davis and isolated one-offs like Blue Train on Blue Note. My usual listening choices run the gamut from the Prestige and Atlantic recordings (especially Olé , the last of them, with Freddie Hubbard, Eric Dolphy and Art Davis added to the working quartet of McCoy Tyner, Reggie Workman and Elvin Jones). My listening range ends with one of my favorites, Meditations , with the “classic” quartet augmented by Rashied Ali and Pharoah Sanders. I hardly ever, if at all, listen to much that came later. Whether that’s because the actual experience of the last quintet live was enough – sufficiently intense -- to satisfy my need for that music, or that the music is so unstable or destabilizing that I don’t feel a need to hear it in its “frozen” form. The sole exception made among recordings of the last stage is Interstellar Space , the recording of four duets with Rashied Ali, recorded in February 1967, though it too is rarely played, singled out perhaps for the relative coherence of the music and the focus of its intensity. © Stuart Broomer, 2026 Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

It takes you through so many emotions, it can make you angry, it's bluesy, it's funny at parts (has a track on dedicated to a candy bar).But man, although the musicianship is of course fantastic, Captain's vocal performance makes the real difference here. Just listen to songs like "Where there's woman" , "Grown so ugly", "Autumn's child", or "Electricity" (where he literally broke a microphone while recording it.)Although Zappa was a good friend and inspiration to Captain Beefheart, Captain's music is far more accessible and this album is a good starting point for a listener who wants to discover their music.
items._cn_summary: 这张1967年的专辑融合了蓝调与迷幻摇滚元素，却突破了常规形式，向前卫与实验方向延伸。乐评指出专辑邀请了多位优秀乐手参与，编曲扎实且演奏水准极高，但真正让作品与众不同的是主唱Captain Beefheart的嗓音表现——他在录音时甚至曾唱断麦克风，展现出原始而强烈的情感冲击力。歌词内容跨度广泛，从对女性的感悟、成长的苦涩，到向一块糖果致敬的诙谐曲目，情绪层次丰富。整张专辑节奏流畅、可听性强，既保留了蓝调的根基，又渗透着实验性色彩。作为Captain Beefheart与Frank Zappa友谊的见证，作品在前卫框架内保持了相当的可接近性，被乐评视为进入其音乐世界的良好起点。

Thankfully, through its
items.body: John Coltrane - One Down, One Up: Live At the Half Note (recorded 1965, released 2005), My Favorite Things: Coltrane At Newport (recorded 1963 and 1965, released 2007), Offering: Live At Temple University (recorded 1966, released 2014), A Love Supreme: Live In Seattle (recorded 1965, released 2021), Evenings At the Village Gate: John Coltrane with Eric Dolphy (recorded 1961, released 2023) By Lee Rice Epstein 1965 was remarkably transformative year in Coltrane’s history. Thankfully, through its ongoing archival releases, Impulse Records has continued to fill in the picture of how, as an artist, he continually pushed himself and his band, deeply and passionately giving his all at all times. One Down, One Up takes us right to March 26, 1965, where Coltrane, McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison, and Elvin Jones play an astonishingly high-wire, high-energy “One Down, One Up” that runs nearly 30 minutes. The electricity crackling between players says exactly why Coltrane still matters, why he’s still adored, and why countless players of all kinds continue to study and revere him. The set’s recapitulation on the Newport stage months later (the second half of My Favorite Things: Coltrane At Newport ), more clearly shows how the group was thinking about and working through their headiest ideas. That the Newport set was released with a 1963 performance featuring Roy Haynes in the drummer seat gives some additional dimensions to the quartet’s changes over time. Tyner and Jones moved on by the next year, while Garrison held down the Alice Coltrane, Rashied Ali, and Pharoah Sanders group. Reportedly, he didn’t play with them in the fall of 1966, when Coltrane led a phenomenal set at Temple University. Offering has been alternately reviled and lauded, cited by some as a polished but unnecessary bootleg for completists only. But, if one just takes a step back and considers Offering happening the same season as Albert Ayler’s seminal European tour—with the quintet of Ayler, Donald Ayler, Michel Samson, Bill Folwell, and Beaver Harris—and if one wants to get really interested in sympathetic wavelengths, you hear Coltrane singing reportedly for the first time ever during “Leo” on November 11, 1966, while Ayler was recorded doing the same on a performance of Sanders’s “Japan” the previous night, November 10, 1966. That Ayler later screamed during his memorial performance for Coltrane would be too on the nose if someone manufactured it. The two shared both intellectual and spiritual bonds, a beautiful thing we’re scarcely able to know of or understand even partly. As the saying goes, it would have been enough to get these first three albums, but the 2020s has produced two seemingly impossible sessions: a live recording of “A Love Supreme,” also from 1965, and an unissued session with Eric Dolphy from 1961, featuring “Greensleeves” and “Africa.” What, truly can be said about Coltrane and Dolphy that doesn’t lead to a mountain of what-if or if-only hypotheticals? The hour-plus set is fiery and rich with ideas in motion. If someone told me this was 1963 or ’64, I wouldn’t doubt it. By ’61, both Coltrane and Dolphy were already well out in front of many contemporaries, and the mutual support demonstrated during their brief time together is beautifully realized here. On A Love Supreme (fascinatingly, recorded a couple days after Live In Seattle), Coltrane leads a kind of crossover group, with Tyner, Garrison, and Jones as the core quartet, joined on the tour by Sanders and Donald Garrett on bass, with Carlos Ward jumping in on sax at Coltrane’s invitation. Both Coltrane and Sanders add percussion along with Jones’s drumming, and if Offering represents some kind of approaching end point in Coltrane’s art, the Seattle performance of “A Love Supreme” leads in the same direction, ever forward. items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评聚焦于Impulse厂牌近年陆续发行的John Coltrane档案录音，跨越1961至1966年的多个现场演出。乐评详细梳理了Coltrane经典四重奏在1965年Half Note俱乐部的高能即兴，以及同组曲目在Newport音乐节舞台上的演变与重塑。Temple University现场记录了Coltrane与Alice Coltrane、Rashied Ali、Pharoah Sanders合作阶段的激烈转变，并与同期Albert Ayler的欧洲巡演形成精神层面的呼应——两位音乐家在相近时间开始以人声作为乐器进行探索，体现出自由爵士在六十年代中后期的精神性突破。乐评还讨论了2020年代面世的1965年《A Love Supreme》现场版以及1961年与Eric Dolphy合作的未发行录音，后者包含《Greensleeves》与《Africa》两首作品，为爵士史提供了珍贵的档案文献。整体而言，乐评以学术化的视角串联起这些现场录音的历史脉络与艺术价值。

items.body: Label: Burning Ambulance Records, 2026 Personnel - Wadada Leo Smith: trumpet; Sylvie Courvoisier: piano (#1,3); Marcus Gilmore: drums (#1,3); Bobby Naughton: vibraphone (#2-5); Lamar Smith: electric guitar (#2,3,5); Bill Laswell: electric bass (#3,4); Melvin Gibbs: electric bass (#3,4); Mauro Refosco: percussion (#2,3,5); Brian Jawara Gray: percussion (#2,3,5); Pheeroan akLaff: drums (#2-5). Trumpeter and composer Wadada Leo Smith assembled various ensembles for his new album, Constellations and Hemispheres , rooted in harmonic intensity, open structures, and modal depth. The project was sparked by quantum physics, parallel universes, and shifting dimensions, in a no-nonsense approach that explores timbre and atmosphere with serious intentions and exceptional versatility. The album kicks off in trio format, with Smith joining forces with the quick-witted pianist Sylvie Courvoisier and adaptable drummer Marcus Gilmore on “ Dark Energy ”. Cymbal activity is paired with sparse piano texture, while Smith's declamations extend from sharply piercing to dolefully lugubrious. This mournful reflection swells and intensifies via Courvoisier's phenomenal work, expanding and contracting by way of intricately coiling patterns that work as a perfect foil for Smith's obscure idioms. Gilmore is granted a brief unaccompanied passage. " Lake Tanganyika " emerged from a sextet session with trumpet, vibraphone, guitar, percussion, and drums. Ancient, water-surrounded landscapes are evoked via the emotionally powerful lyricism brought by Smith over Bobby Naughton's gossamer vibes and Pheeroan AkLaff's gloriously relentless drum flow. The seasoned drummer also gets our attention on the closer, " Meditation on Love ", a cosmic, open-ended manifesto of peace and hope. Smith traces a spiritual and artistic connection with the Rastafari—associated with the reggae music of Jamaica—but I'm unable to spot that influence here. Yet the music is able to knife through the speakers like a lightning bolt. " Dark Matters, Particles of Light, Mirror of the Unseen " is a full-length workout clocking in at 22 minutes. Powerful and moody, the piece is bookended by the same trio that had shaped the opening track, expanding in its middle part into an octet featuring two distinguished electric bassists, Bill Laswell and Melvin Gibbs, who contribute to the dismal, apocalyptic scenario with authority. A lighter, tactile percussive quality appears by the end, relieving the pressure. The two bassists are also prominent on " Deep Canyons on Mars ", diffusing ominous vibes through gravelly distorted sounds. The heavy, nightmarish tones are pacified when vibraphone and trumpet step forward, yet obscurity still lives here when the bass returns with wah-wah bluesy sounds drowned in electronics. Though the result of multiple sessions, Constellations and Hemispheres feels like a unified experiment—mostly stripped down of gloss but still with haunting and transcendent moments to reflect upon. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Dark Energy ► 02 - Lake Tanganyika ► 03 - Dark Matters, Particles of Light, Mirror of the Unseen
items._cn_summary: Wadada Leo Smith 的新专辑《Constellations and Hemispheres》以量子物理学、平行宇宙与维度转换为灵感来源，汇集多组不同编制展开实验。专辑以三重奏开场，史密斯的小号与钢琴、鼓形成张力对话，稀疏织体中透出尖锐与忧郁的交替。中段加入电贝斯、颤音琴与多重打击乐，乐句在开放结构中自由延展。长达22分钟的核心曲目由三重奏扩展为八重奏，两把电贝斯以失真音效营造末日般沉重氛围，尾部以更轻盈的打击乐质感释放压力。全作虽来自多次录音，却被整合为一个统一的声学实验——剥离修饰，保留阴郁与超越交织的时刻，在器乐即兴与宇宙意象之间建立联系。

items.body:
Curating a retrospective of 40 years of recorded music is a daunting task, particularly when it is your own. Accurately representing the arc of the work and the life that created it requires frankness and acceptance. It is a process punctuated with winces and sighs and the occasional grin. Composer and improviser Jin Hi Kim experienced it all when compiling The Jin Hi Kim Collection, recently issued by Neuma. If the use of “odyssey” requires a great voyage, discovering new lands, and encountering titans, then Kim’s journey easily qualifies. Not only did she leave Korea at 23 for the US in 1980, Kim traversed an arguably greater gulf by leaving her elite training in traditional Korean music to study electronic music and composition with Lou Harrison, Terry Riley, and others. In the intervening decades, she worked with leading exponents of contemporary composition and improvisation like Kronos Quartet and Derek Bailey, and transformed the komungo, the traditional five-foot-long lute dating from the 4th Century CE, exponentially extending its sonic range through computer interfaces and signal processing.

Rediscovery accompanied the selection process for the 9-CD Collection. She was especially surprised when reviewing early works transliterating Korean music through Western instruments, or employing graphic notation. “It was created by a young mind,” Kim recently recalled with a laugh. “Sometimes it was hard to hear that’s what I did. But it was also good evidence for an archival collection. It was a wonderful feeling to look at everything I did – well, almost everything – but one thing that I was really proud about it is that there is not just one kind of music. Each piece has its Korean roots but, like I’ve said, I came to America to make new music, so I look at my 40 years of work and, yeah, I achieved that. So, it was a very satisfying process.

“When I listen to some of the improvisations, I realized how young and unafraid I was. Komungo has a limited sound compared to other instruments. When you work with virtuoso improvisers, they have vocabularies that are so rich. They are creating so many different colors and textures, but komungo has limits. It doesn’t allow you to express so much of the story. It has a meditative energy, of nothingness, of slowness. I was so brave to use this instrument with such incredible masters and to communicate with them and create music with them. I did it somehow with my inner energy. I was able to present this inner energy.”

The Collection almost equally divides Kim’s work in composition and improvisation, with five discs devoted to works for orchestra and chamber music ensembles, and four documenting improvisations with, among others, an impressive diversity of percussionists, including Gerry Hemingway, Susie Ibarra, and Tony Oxley, and string players like Bill Frisell, Min Xiao-Fen, and Hans Reichel. If anything can be read into it, the slight tilt reflects her ardent pursuit to articulate the concept of Living Tones Compositions, and how central it is to her work.

“The most important thing about the Living Tones Compositions is to convey the Korean element and philosophy through Western contemporary music,” she explained. “When I came to the United States after training in traditional Korean music, European classical music was more respected in Korea than the traditional music. They didn’t know much about American avant-garde music then, in the 1970s. I was a young musician who trained with the very best teachers and saw that I was not respected because I was not doing Western music.

“That created within me a great desire to fix that problem. You can’t fix anything, but I was young, I had a passion and a mission. I was living in the United States; I was composing for Western musicians; so how could I make this Korean idea, this Korean state of mind in making music, how could I put this together with Western music with equal respect? That was my thing. All my Living Tones Compositions come from the idea of putting together the Korean context and philosophy and Western instruments and musical context, to see how Western musicians took to the Korean attitude – not necessarily techniques, scales, anything like that – but this attitude, this state of mind. That’s what I’m doing with Living Tones music.

“Korean traditional music was once influenced by Chinese music,” Kim prefaced to explain the context and philosophy of Korean music, which she also detailed extensively in her book, Duality of Ancient Korean Roots and Western New Music. “Korean music can be divided into folk music and court music. Court music was quite different from music of ordinary people. The court was deeply influenced by ancient Chinese philosophy – yin and yang; the five elements, and ancient ancestors worship. The music wasn’t entertainment; it was ritual – that was part of both court and folk music. For ordinary people, they associated music with the shaman. For court music, there were virtuoso musicians who created an austere music, based on a philosophy of cosmic sound and abstract thinking; but for ordinary people, the shaman always took care of pain, community pain. Music was performed for celebrations of harvests and other things, but more for problems like drought, someone who is sick, some kind of problem. The shaman is always dealing with the problem of pain in their lives. They always had to sing something very sad. Her song has nothing to do with joyous things – always grief and pain. Ordinary people related to that.

“Both court and folk music had an emphasis on energy – they never thought of music as just sound. It had healing energy. In the folk community, they tried to imitate the shaman, the way she sang, shaking the notes, trying to reach out to another spirit, trying to connect heaven and earth. If you listen to a shaman’s song, there’s a very strong vibrato. The instrumentalists who don’t sing listen to this type of music; it’s very touching, very soulful, and it reflects the problems in their lives. Korean instrumentalists are all shaking, shaking their hands, shaking their instruments, shaking their notes. I play komungo, where the strings can move a lot, up and down, so you can really shake the notes and express the music in the same way as the shaman. I translate that process, that context, that spirit, into Living Tones. Each tone has its own light, and because it has its own light, its time is elastic. It is not like abstract Western time, where you count the time of each note perfectly, and you don’t have the space for microtones. There’s no time to do that in Western music. Time becomes much more open and that’s why in Korean music they don’t talk about abstract time but time in a cycle. Within that cycle, you have a lot of freedom of how to use that space with deep vibratos or any other articulation to create that intense feeling.”

The qualities Kim ascribes to Korean music are manifest in the komungo. It has a palpably plangent sound, with a bass register lower and more resonant than the guembri’s and the sting of ancient harps in its highest notes. It has a timbral luster comparable to the dark, iridescent glazes of pit-fired ceramics or the blocks of deep color that hover over the black basecoats of a Mark Rothko painting. Its dredge-like twang and the skeletal figures central to the music stop the racing, associative Western mind dead in its tracks. Even before Kim augmented the instrument with signal processing, Western improvisers had a strong attraction to the komungo. Conversely, improvisation has, over the decades, impacted Kim’s outlook.

However, Kim has a nuanced view on how improvisation has influenced her. “Influence is the result over a long period,” she elaborated, “because I played with a person one time or two times. That long period is a really deep space. It’s not that a particular musician gave me something. It is that the experience of playing with someone becomes part of my life experience. Now I look at something differently than when I was young. I understand how the universe works because of scientists and I understand how improvisation works because of improvisers. When you travel all around the world – I’ve performed in over 60 countries and have lived in some of these countries for a long time, six months or even a year – then you have an incredibly different life perspective. All of those things interest me. So, I have been influenced by many things over the decades, so that when I play with someone, it is not just that moment I am responding to; it’s everything about the other musicians: their instruments; their traditions; their culture. That gives me a very clear idea what to do.

“When I was young, I was so desperate to communicate successfully with each improviser I played with. I was trying to understand their personality; I was trying to understand their vocabulary. There have been very few times that I played on the spot without any information about the people I was playing with. I had heard them before I had the opportunity to play with them, playing with other musicians or solo. In my own way, I understood who they are. If I don’t understand them and their musical elements, I have no way to contribute anything on komungo. I have to understand their personality, their energy, how they process the music. Not all people process the same way; some people are poetic; some people are very emotional; some people are very funny. Everybody has those things happening. Understanding that was very important to me. It helped me to communicate, to hear what they were giving me, so I could give back. I listened a lot to what they were doing at a particular moment.”

Given that improvisers spanning James Newton and Elliott Sharp, and Rüdiger Carl and Oliver Lake, are heard throughout the box set, it is noteworthy that Kim singles one out to illustrate her approach to improvisation. “When I work with William Parker, he has a very deep energy in his soul,” she said of the bassist. “When I played with him, he influenced me with his deep energy. It’s really big. That influenced me to be really big. That bigness, that abundance, that tireless energy; that lets us play a really long time. He has the qualities to do something that a Korean shaman could do, playing the same idea over and over and over for a long time – trance like – but the energy becomes more powerful. William Parker has that type of energy. The bass is like the komungo; it has a deep energy and incredible power. I’m really influenced by that.”

Retrospectives like the Collection are generally considered to be merely summations, but in Kim’s case, it is more a marker of distance travelled and journeys ahead. “It reflects my continuous evolution as an artist. Throughout my musical journey, I have always searched for new ways to express myself creatively while remaining deeply rooted in my Korean musical identity.

“In essence, every work in this collection is the result of my enduring desire to elevate often-neglected Korean aesthetics, shaped alongside the freedom I found in America – a place that allowed me to pursue my artistic passions and ideas without limitation.

“Today, my perspective extends beyond national boundaries to the increasingly interconnected global community. I have aspired to use music as a spiritual and transformative force to confront social challenges. I believe this has become the new direction of my artistic journey.”

Kim’s new direction has steered her towards to uplifting marginalized subalterns and breaking through the fourth wall of the concert hall separating musicians from listeners. “Right now, because the world has changed so much, and America is now so blue, and so many people are mentally ill – I know because I recently gave a music meditation workshop at the Yale mental health center – I want to do something about community pain. I always go back to what the shaman does. I think I have sort of achieved my goal of blending Korean and Western ways of thinking with Living Tones, so right now I want to make music that the community participates in. Not necessarily well-trained musicians, but anybody who is interested. I already started on this in 2023 with a piece called ‘Ritual for Earth.’ I would like to do these things for now. I’m not anxious about my career or my next commission. I’m thinking about community pain, environmental issues like wildfires and floods, the world we are living in. So, if I have the opportunity, working with communities is what I want to do.”
items._cn_summary: 本乐评介绍韩裔作曲家兼即兴演奏家Jin Hi Kim的9CD作品合集，收录其四十年创作生涯的精选。Kim自幼接受韩国传统音乐训练，赴美后转向电子音乐与作曲，师从Lou Harrison与Terry Riley，并长期与Kronos Quartet、Derek Bailey等当代音乐名家合作。其最具突破性的贡献在于将拥有四百年历史的传统乐器玄琴与现代技术融合，通过计算机接口与信号处理极大扩展其音色边界。合集均衡呈现其作曲与即兴创作：五张碟收录管弦乐与室内乐作品，四张碟记录与Gerry Hemingway、Susie Ibarra、Tony Oxley等打击乐手及Bill Frisell、Min Xiao-Fen等弦乐演奏家的即兴合作。Kim的创作始终扎根于韩国传统，却持续拓展新的音乐语言，体现了跨文化、跨类型的持续探索精神。
