items.body:
Live at Rockpalast 1999
documents a command performance at the Loreley open-air amphitheater by Malcolm �Mac� Rebennack Jr., aka Dr. John. Rockpalast is a live-music TV show broadcast since 1974 by Westdeutscher Rundfunk (WDR), the archival source for this CD-DVD package, and coincidentally a remarkable cultural institution on its own terms.
Taped at the height of Dr. John�s international popularity, backing the singer-pianist-guitarist are New Orleans stalwarts Bobby Broom (guitar), David Barard (bass), and Herman Ernest (drums), a tight quartet that projects authority and engages the crowd from start to close.
A striking UNESCO-designated World Heritage Site set, the Loreley is a slate pinnacle on a mythic horseshoe bend of the Rhine River, memorializing an enduring German literary legend both tragic and romantic. The setting is thus well-suited for Mac�s mystical spirit and lyrical style. By this stage of his career, he characterized his live show as a Mardi Gras revue with a mix of New Orleans standards and some of his most recognizable compositions.
Hence, he opens with the NOLA classic �Iko, Iko,� a half-sung, half-chanted celebration of community participation in the renowned Mardi Gras second-line street procession. Then comes the in-your-face boast �Qualified,� wherein the singer warns, �I got the power to control / I can see clean through you, blind mole / I want to tell you now, I'm qualified / You know that I'm qualified.�
Any Dr. John fan will recognize �I Walk on Guilded Splinters,� a moody, percussively insistent, foreboding expression of the Night Tripper�s immersion in �funknology� (his term), gris-gris herbology, and hoodoo incantation, punctuated with jungle growls and cries, a loopy, spooky slide whistle, and an extended psych-guitar solo: �Walk thru the fire / Fly thru the smoke / See my enemy / At the end of dey rope.�
Every piece in this well- honed set deserves considertion. Although Dr John lived for many years in Los Angeles and New York, his enduring hometown connection shows in the fond inclusion of his own �Sweet Home New Orleans� and �Goin� Back to New Orleans,� and he nods to a key influence with a funky rendering of Duke Ellington�s �I'm Gonna Go Fishin�.� Among other gems are Mac�s Top�10 hit �Right Place, Wrong Time,� and the instantly recognizable closer, Earl King�s �Big Chief,� another Mardi Gras burner.
Regarding his live performance approach, per the notes, �I always play a little bit of everything. I think that�s what music�s about: a little bit of somethin� old, somethin� in the middle, somethin� new, and somethin� as yet uncreated.�
Dr John's�s longtime fans will welcome this archival gem, which also is a solid introduction for any late comers to the party. Surmounting the barriers of language and culture, the power of
At the Rockpalast
is also evident in the enthusiastic audience response. As he declares, �If you�re gonna get off on somethin� you don�t need to know nothin� about it. Music is a universal language.�

items._cn_summary: 这张现场专辑记录了Dr. John于1999年在德国莱茵河畔洛雷莱露天剧场的演出，由西德意志广播公司WDR的长期音乐节目Rockpalast录制发行。乐队以钢琴为核心，伴以吉他、贝斯和鼓的紧凑编制，演绎了新奥尔良风格的放克与节奏蓝调曲目。开场以经典的'Iko Iko'引入狂欢节气氛，随后展开包含'Qualified'、'I Walk on Guilded Splinters'等代表作的完整曲目，融合巫毒仪式意象与迷幻放克元素。专辑还致敬杜克·艾灵顿等前辈，收录Earl King的'Big Chief'作为终曲。对于新奥尔良音乐爱好者而言，这是一次具有地域文化深度的现场记录，但对实验或前卫音乐取向的听众来说，传统布鲁斯与放克的根基限制了其创新空间。

items.body: Review by martindavey87 — 'Pulse For a Graveheart' is the second studio album by Italian progressive metal band Mind Key. Released in 2009, the group has shown a significant improvement over the four years that had passed since their debut, with stronger writing and a better-sounding production, a high quality is consistently maintained throughout the album. One major change in the bands line-up is the addition of new vocalist Aurelio Fierro. Former singer Marco Basile had a fantastic range, but at times his voice seemed quite tinny, whereas Fierro's powerful voice fits more comfortably with the music, adapting for soft, melodic sections or heavier, more aggressive parts. As expected with this genre, the musicianship is fantastic as always, featuring plenty of great interplay between all the instruments, with particular praise going to guitarist Emanuele Colella and keyboardist Dario De Cicco. There's also guest appearances by the likes of keyboard maestro Derek Sherinian, Tom Englund (of Everygrey fame), and Winger's Reb Beach.With highlights including 'Sunset Highway', 'Dead Fame Hunter', 'The Seventh Seal', 'Citizen of Greed' and 'Graveheart', this is a solid progressive metal album and sure to please all fans of the genre.

items.excerpt: Review by Fercandio46 — The use of synthesizers and the Mellotron, combined with an abrasive, dense hard rock sound, defined Black Bonzo's debut as progressive hard rock; vocalist Magnus Lindgren, with his very clean voice, and keyboardist Nicklas Ahlund, capable of playing everything from rock 'n' roll to classical organ passages, evoke the more daring side of Deep Purple, while on the title track, "Lady of the Light," they also create an almost cinematic, eerie atmosphere."Brave Young So
items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The use of synthesizers and the Mellotron, combined with an abrasive, dense hard rock sound, defined Black Bonzo's debut as progressive hard rock; vocalist Magnus Lindgren, with his very clean voice, and keyboardist Nicklas Ahlund, capable of playing everything from rock 'n' roll to classical organ passages, evoke the more daring side of Deep Purple, while on the title track, "Lady of the Light," they also create an almost cinematic, eerie atmosphere."Brave Young Soldier" also features psychedelia, rhythmic shifts, and dissonances that greatly enrich the track; once again, Magnus Lindgren demonstrates his own distinct personality and style, avoiding the path of other singers in the genre. Guitar and organ combine for a brilliant riff at the end, blending a medieval past with rock music evocative of spells and stone forests."Fantasy World" evoked a different atmosphere, reminiscent of Wishbone Ash; "Freedom," on the other hand, could easily have appeared on Queen's debut album. The melody ultimately took center stage, a gothic, operatic tune that kept evolving. While this didn't necessarily contribute to the album's cohesion, the diversity added emotional depth, featuring the Mellotron from "Sirens" and, above all, the drumming, which, combined with the acoustic guitar, recalled King Crimson's debut.On one hand, there is the clenched-teeth rock and tight sound of "Jailbait," and the dark, ominous lyricism of "Leave Your Burdens", complete with Black Sabbath-style riffs reminiscent of their bluesier moments, while the hypnotic conclusion of "Where the River Meets the Sea" serves as the perfect finale. It clearly defines an artistic vision that was at once velvet and steel, possessing scales and gills to dive through the ocean, yet also lungs to scream and fill with air in order to fly.

items.body: Review by DimitrisTheHead — There is something about those late '60s/early '70s English albums, in contrast to the American ones, that make them sound epic. Is it the atmosphere? Is it the lyrics? Is it the keys? Is it something else? Maybe it is all these things combined. Now this record, has all that trademark elements of that era, it's bluesy, it's heavy, it's dark in some moments and happy on other moments, it's progy. "Repent Walpurgis" is an amazing instrumental and one of my favorites from that era. Matthew Fisher on the hammond, give me that same feeling, Jon Lord (Deep Purple) or Ken Hensley (Uriah Heep) give me when I'm listening to their records. Yes lads, it is that good.Procol Harum, as a typical British band, decided to leave "A whiter shade of pale" off of the UK vinyl release and put it just on the North America release, plus they left some amazing songs as bonus tracks. (Just listen "Homburg"!!!)A must listen for the fans of that era.
items._genre: crossover prog / psychedelic rock / blues rock / baroque pop
items._cn_summary: 1967年英国Procol Harum首张专辑将巴洛克元素、布鲁斯与英国六十年代末特有的忧郁氛围相融合。Matthew Fisher的风琴演奏是专辑核心，赋予作品类似Deep Purple与Uriah Heep Hammond风琴主导的史诗感与器乐深度。《Repent Walpurgis》作为器乐曲展现出明显的渐进摇滚倾向，层次推进与阴暗色调兼具。值得关注的是英美版本曲目差异——英国版未收录后来成为经典的《A Whiter Shade of Pale》，而北美版将此曲与《Homburg》等作品作为附赠收录，反映了当时跨大西洋唱片发行的差异策略。整体制作偏向传统英式摇滚框架，虽有实验性编排但仍属主流摇滚语境下的风格融合，与前卫实验路线存在较大距离。

items.body: Review by Warthur — Bakerloo's sole album reveals them as a truly diverse progressive group of the early prog era. They've clearly emerged from the same blues rock primordial soup formented by the Yardbirds and Bluesbreakers and Cream and which saw peers like Jetbro Tull and Black Sabbath emerge. Bakerloo actually shared a manager with Sabbath, but it's Tull who you'll be reminded of most - in particular, the sound of their earliest days, before Mick Abrahams left. There's no flute, but plenty of harmonica - and the power trip work in enough influences from jazz and classical music to suggest a group just as broad in influences as Tull, though perhaps with more influence from the calmer, more meditative side of psychedelia creeping in at points.It's no surprise that they fell by the wayside at the end - this was a crowded scene, after all, and it was all too easy for groups to get lost in the shuffle, and with Tull already evolving away from their early blues influences and Black Sabbath turning the blues into doom metal their peers were moving to distinguish themselves, so you can see why Bakerloo were in danger of being eclipsed. In retrospect, it's a gem of its particular scene - it's just that the scene in question was on the cusp of being overtaken by other strands of prog and blues-derived rock.
items._genre: proto-prog / blues rock / psychedelic rock / jazz-rock
items._cn_summary: 这是Bakerloo乐队唯一的专辑，诞生于1969年前卫摇滚萌芽时期。乐队从布鲁斯摇滚土壤中生长出来，吸收了Yardbirds、Bluesbreakers、Cream等前辈的影响，同时融入了爵士与古典元素，整体风格与早期Jethro Tull颇为相似——以口琴代替长笛，音色偏向迷幻氛围中较为沉静冥想的一面。评论将这张专辑定位为那个特定场景的宝石，但同时指出其同侪如Jethro Tull与Black Sabbath已各自走向更鲜明的演化方向，使Bakerloo在激烈竞争中逐渐被边缘化。专辑展现出广泛的音乐素养，但在开创性上未能走出独立的辨识度，最终沦为时代过渡期的产物。

items.body: Review by sgtpepper — After a long-term hiatus (last good album released in 1981), Collegium Musicum returned at least to the stage in 1997 with the original members of which Freso remained in a particular good shape. The choice of tracks performed was good as it didn't only feature the first two albums but reached later into their career. I am personally a bigger fan of their 1971-1975 period rather than their first eponymous album.The guest Andrej Seban provides elastic guitar while Hajek hasn't lost his edge on the drums.I'm not very content with Varga though because I find his playing somehow sloppy - as if he couldn't hit all the right keys, or not always on time. This suspicion raised with me in the beginning of the first track but hasn't evaporated later. Or is it just the not keyboard sound which does not allow for careful key distinction?In any case, this was the first official live album with their classic songs, however the double live album from 2010 could be more appealing.
items._genre: symphonic prog / progressive rock / live album
items._cn_summary: 斯洛伐克乐队Collegium Musicum沉寂多年后于1997年重组回归舞台，本作收录了此次重组演出的现场录音。曲目跨越乐队职业生涯，涵盖早期两张专辑及后期作品。评论指出鼓手Hajek依然锋利，吉他手Freso状态良好，特邀嘉宾Andrej Seban的吉他演奏富有弹性。然而主创Varga的键盘表现被认为不够精准，常有滑键或节奏偏差的问题，声音本身的混响也加重了这一缺陷。作为乐队的首张官方现场专辑，其意义大于演奏本身的完成度；2010年的双碟现场录音被认为是更理想的选择。整体演出更偏向怀旧回顾，而非艺术突破。

items.body: Metanoia, Yulianna Avdeeva’s new album for Pentatone, focuses on the transformation of Liszt’s style between his Weimar and late periods. Liszt had already shown an experimental curiosity with structure and form in the Sonata in B minor—a work presented here alongside later pieces such as the Bagatelle sans tonalité and Nuages gris. Metanoia Amazon Presto Apple Given the many versions available, Avdeeva’s B minor sonata is impressive. Some renditions are either entirely too heavy or too light, but hers strikes a sensible balance of power, speed, and musicality. There are admittedly some moments where velocity comes at the expense of clarity, but the furious and urgent spirit is aptly captured. Avdeeva shows firm command in the first section (track 1). The octave passages are bold and brash, while the runs remain light, agile, and effortless. I did find the lead-up to the second theme somewhat rushed: the Grandioso (track 2) is rousing but needs more breadth for us to fully appreciate the arrival of the D major section—something Argerich’s 1971 recording does so well. The more tender moments of the section, however, are exquisitely rendered with translucent passagework. Fortunately, Avdeeva does not rush the Andante (track 3). Its blend of nostalgia, reverie, and introspection offers a much-needed respite from the frenetic parts of the sonata and leaves enough space for the return of drama in the finale. The fugue (track 4), meticulous in its rhythm and articulation, gives a powerful drive back to the recapitulation but never leaves us with any sense of uncomfortable volatility. The late works begin with La lugubre gondola II (track 5), whose origins are as dark as the music. In 1882, Liszt is said to have had an eerie vision that his son-in-law Richard Wagner would die and that his body would be carried on a black gondola. The vision came true a few months later, in early 1883. Avdeeva reflects the grim nature of this realization as she highlights the starkness of the sparse textures and the austerity, foreboding, and finality of the monophony. The work is as much an homage to Wagner as it is a premonition, and the second half is where we hear more elements of tonality and lyricism. R.W. – Venezia (track 9), the companion work to La lugubre gondola, was written after Wagner’s death. While just as somber and still minimalistic, the piece lies largely in the lower register. Avdeeva gives the left-hand octave ostinato plenty of depth but also a necessary sense of severity. The brighter Bagatelle sans tonalité (track 6) recalls the showmanship of earlier works, though the bravado now takes the form of a more elegant virtuosity. The unmistakable element of caprice is well evoked. Yulianna Avdeeva. Photo © Kevin Kinzley. Nuages gris (track 7), like La lugubre gondola, has sinister undertones amid its minimalism. Avdeeva still finds a way to create some breathtaking tone colors; the final two mysterious chords are a good example, offering a fleeting sense of whimsy quite different from the ominous mood that pervades most of the piece. The Hungarian Rhapsody No. 17 (track 10), written just a few years before Liszt’s death, diverges considerably in character from the earlier rhapsodies, Nos. 1–15. The flamboyant, fiery, and playful profile gives way to more ominous undertones and an atonal base. Avdeeva brings out a threatening and even aggressive nature: accents and dissonances carry a stinging sharpness, and the octave passages at the end are adamant and tumultuous. Unstern! – Sinistre (track 11) is perhaps the most jarring of the late pieces, owing to its harsh atonality and even harsher textures. The accents and chords here are abrasive (as they should be), yet never become too strident on the ears. Unlike some of the other works, whose endings offer some form of catharsis, the latter sections here only prolong the doubt and disquiet, a distinction Avdeeva makes clear. The juxtaposition of works from different eras is well judged. In one sitting, the heavy mood of the late works may become a bit overbearing, but this only goes to show the effectiveness of Avdeeva’s interpretations. All in all, a series of excellent performances that should find a place on the shelf of any Liszt enthusiast. items.body: Seattle darkwave project The Phantom Eyes released a video for its cover of DEVO’s “Puppet Boy,” directed by Tori Kellogg (credited as GR4VES), on 25 September 2026. DEVO’s original “Puppet Boy” appeared on the 1984 album “Shout.” The Phantom Eyes is the recording name of Bex Delgado, who released the cover in May 2026 before the video followed in September. Puppet Boy by The Phantom Eyes The Phantom Eyes’ video for ‘Puppet Boy’ Kellogg filmed the video in a single evening, building the look around red lighting, CRT distortion and VHS-style degradation. Delgado described the story behind the cover: “I was trying to embody the spirit of not exactly a dom/sub relationship, but more like a master/servant one. This story isn’t romantic in nature, but still has that sweet feeling that the characters do take care of each other.” About The Phantom Eyes The Phantom Eyes is the Seattle-based recording project of Bex Delgado, mixes darkwave and dark electronic music with post-punk elements. Delgado describes the project’s focus as horror, isolation and existential dread. The cover of DEVO’s “Puppet Boy,” released in May 2026, is one of the project’s singles; its video, filmed by Tori Kellogg and released 25 September 2026, is the most recent visual release under the project’s name.
items._cn_summary: 西雅图暗潮项目The Phantom Eyes由Bex Delgado主理，2026年5月发行了DEVO 1984年专辑《Shout》中《Puppet Boy》的翻唱版本，9月25日释出由Tori Kellogg（署名GR4VES）执导的MV。视频在一个晚上完成拍摄，以红色灯光、CRT失真与VHS风格画面退化构建视觉氛围。Delgado将翻唱的叙事诠释为一种非浪漫的主仆关系，强调角色间的照护意味。音乐层面，该项目融合暗潮、暗电子与后朋克元素，主题聚焦恐怖、孤立与存在主义焦虑。然而原文本质上是一篇新闻资讯稿而非深度乐评，缺乏对声音设计、编曲结构、翻唱与原作差异等音乐性层面的具体分析，信息密度有限，难以对作品的艺术价值做出有效判断。

items.body: West Palm Beach dance-punk trio Violet Silhouette released the single “This Is Something” on 25 September 2026, with a video directed by Roberto Badillo. The track pairs post-punk structures with dance rhythms, with reference points close to early Human League and LCD Soundsystem. Violet Silhouette is Dan, Zaii and Lily Vile (bass), formed in West Palm Beach, Florida in late 2019 and now based between South Florida and Austin, Texas. This Is Something by Violet Silhouette Violet Silhouette’s video for ‘This Is Something’ Roberto Badillo directed the video for “This Is Something,” which the band says draws on David Lynch’s 1997 film “Lost Highway.” Violet Silhouette described the concept: “Visually, we drew from David Lynch’s Lost Highway. Our friend Roberto Badillo took our vision and ran with it, the result is sleek and visceral, like a gloved hand dragging desire across the table.” About Violet Silhouette Violet Silhouette formed in West Palm Beach, Florida in late 2019. The band is Dan, Zaii and Lily Vile (bass), now split between South Florida and Austin, Texas. Prior releases include the single “Strange Wind” and “Hierda Demonica,” a track from a second EP, alongside the “Feverblue” release on the band’s Bandcamp page. Violet Silhouette has been producing a debut full-length, “VIVID(IS)DECAY,” entirely in-house since 2024. “This Is Something,” released 25 September 2026, is the band’s latest single. Its video, directed by Roberto Badillo, is the most recent visual release tied to the band’s upcoming album.
items._cn_summary: 西棕榈滩三人组合 Violet Silhouette 发行单曲《This Is Something》，将后朋克结构与舞曲节奏相结合，参考早期 Human League 和 LCD Soundsystem 的音乐语汇。乐队由 Dan、Zaii 和贝斯手 Lily Vile 组成，2019 年底成立于佛罗里达，目前活动于南佛罗里达与奥斯汀之间。此前曾发行单曲《Strange Wind》和第二张 EP 中的《Hierda Demonica》，以及 Bandcamp 上的《Feverblue》。自 2024 年起乐队一直自主制作首张全长专辑《VIVID(IS)DECAY》，本作为该专辑的最新单曲。MV 由 Roberto Badillo 执导，视觉灵感取自大卫·林奇 1997 年的电影《Lost Highway》，乐队形容其效果光滑而具肉感，如同一只戴着手套的手将欲望拖过桌面。整体内容更接近新闻稿性质，对音乐本身的听觉细节与制作分析着墨较少。

items._cn_summary: The Flaming Lips 即将发行 2006 年专辑《At War With The Mystics》二十周年豪华盒装再版，收录 19 首未发表 demo、14 首未发表录音室作品以及 42 首非专辑曲目，CD 版本还附有 2007 年现场电影《U.F.O.s At The Zoo》及好莱坞露天剧场演唱会的音频记录。作为继大获成功的《Yoshimi Battles The Pink Robots》四年后推出的第十一张录音室专辑，该作相比前作更偏向吉他驱动的风格方向。再版规模庞大，包含 6CD 与 6LP 多种格式。文章整体为资讯性新闻稿，内容偏向发行信息介绍，缺乏对音乐本身的深度评论或艺术分析。

items.body: Review by yarstruly — TAKEN FROM MY REVIEW ON MY BLOG "SCOTT'S SONG BY SONG SPOTLIGHTS" Which has links for purchasing, and more.Clicked 5, but really a 4.75The prolific UK composer and keyboardist Clive Nolan may be best known as the keyboardist in Pendragon and Arena (see my spotlight on Arena on this blog), but he has really done so much more! He is also part of the bands Shadowland and (formerly) Strangers on a Train. Furthermore, he has a bachelors and masters degree from the London College of Music, and has written, produced and staged musical theater productions with his Caamora Theatre Company. He has also been a part of numerous collaborations, including three albums with Oliver Wakeman. The man is a musical mastermind. His latest solo project "Song of the Winter Throne", due to be released on Friday October 2, is a massive undertaking. It consists of a main CD and a Bonus CD totaling approximately 2 hours in length. The subject of this concept album is H�kon H�konarson, aka Hakon IV, or Hakon the Old. He was a Norwegian King born in 1204, and reigning between 1217-1263, a whopping 46 years! (Interestingly, a Norwegian musician, whose band The Windmill also has been given a Spotlight, Morten L. Clason assisted Clive Nolan in engineering the album.) As H�kon H�konarson ascended to the crown at the age of 13, he was initially King in name only and regent Earl Skule B�rdsson pulled the strings until H�kon reached adulthood. However, B�rdsson would later declare himself king even as H�kon was still on the throne. The true king would have the usurper executed in 1240 and continued his reign. This execution put a close to the long Norwegian Civil War into which H�kon himself was born. His reign is considered to be the zenith of medieval Norwegian civilization.There are a large number of people involved in bringing Clive's musical vision to life. The primary instrumentalists are: Clive Nolan - Keyboards, Orchestration and ProgrammingMirko Sangrigoli - Drums and GuitarsStig Andre' Clason - GuitarsMorten L. Clason - FluteHennie Hagen Johnsen - GuitarsArnfinn Isaksen - BassMeanwhile, the main cast members are:Gemma Ashley - SolveigRyan Morgan - H�kon H�konarsonChristina Booth - TyraClive Nolan - Music & LyricsNatalie Barnett - Freja Ross Andrews - The StorytellerAdditionally, there are 38 members of the chorus, so I will include a picture of that page of the CD booklet, so they get the credit they deserve. (Scroll to the bottom.)Many readers will surely notice the name of Christina Booth, the amazing vocalist of the Band Magenta. Stig Andre' Clason is the son of the aforementioned Morten Clason, who also plays with The Windmill.The album comes courtesy of Anne-Claire of Bad Dog Promotions. As always, I am free to call it as I hear it, and I receive no additional compensation. As per my usual method, this is a cold listen.Obviously, this is a massive production, so let me get on with it and dive into the music!Track 1 - Born in Shadow (3:14)This begins with some sound effects and the narration from Ross Andrews, in dramatic style. Equally dramatic music follows, creating an overture for what is to come. The massive chorus is put to use on this, yet the drums and underlying rhythm keep a rock feel in the music, despite how symphonic it is. A massive opener!Track 2 - The Woman from Varteig (4:34)This begins without a pause from the opener, but the music drops to a drone. Ross Andrews continues the story, discussing the circumstances of H�kon H�konarson's birth. Christina Booth as Tyra sings first, and is joined by both of the other women in their characters. They sing of how they will protect the boy to ensure the safety of the would-be king. Being born "illegitimately" during a civil war was a great danger to the boy. The vocals are flawless and set the tone magnificently. Track 3 - Wolves Gather (3:03)A traditional drum and sound effects accompany Ross Andrews' narration, then foreboding music with chanting enters and then Gemma Ashley and Natalie Barnett sing beautifully in harmony. Power chords from the guitars help to accent the mood of the music.Track 4 - Flight of the Birkebeiners (3:27)The Storyteller continues the saga, then the dramatic music takes over. The string parts are somewhat reminiscent of the piano part on "The Lamb Lies Down on Broadway" (Genesis). The chorus joins in making the scene even more dramatic. Fantastic piece of classical-level music.Track 5 - The Hidden Prince (4:12)The Storyteller continues, then H�kon (Ryan Morgan) joins in for the first time. He sings of the circumstances of his upbringing in the woodlands. A very engaging song!Track 6 - Ritual of Faith (4:29)Ross continues the story, telling of the "Trial by Ordeal" that his mother underwent to prove the boy's lineage and suitableness to become the King. The chorus, along with Tyra and Freja bring the tale to life. A powerful song, fantastically delivered by the amazing cast of musicians Nolan has assembled. Track 7 - The Puppet Crown (4:22)The Storyteller tells us how H�kon was King in Name Only, ruled over by Regents. H�kon sings that it is "The Puppet Crown" along with Solveig. The chorus tells us:This is the puppet Crown,I wear the gold, I wear the gown,But another wields the power,A hand on the hilt of a sword unbound?However, the last line of the song is:"But one day?I'll cut the strings!"The song is probably the catchiest one so far, with lots of power.Track 8 - Fractured Throne (3:40)This song tells of how even after H�kon was King in his own right, his former Regent, Skule B�rdsson, even after being given the title of Duke (the first Duke in Norway), still tried to usurp the Crown and declared himself King?spoilers, It didn't end well for Skule. All of the main characters participate in this song. The song has an air of darkness about it, but H�kon is resolute in saying "I am King, I rule alone!"Track 9 - The Sword and the Fire (6:04)Of course the storyteller starts this one off, and then H�kon and the Chorus perform together on this one. This one describes the civil war battles that finally unified H�kon's power as Skule is executed. Musically there are some odd meters here. Ryan Morgan hits a fantastic sustained high note about halfway through that is fantastic. The resolution portion of the song is so powerful! At the end of this track is the first full stop in the music.Track 10 - A Kingdom Rejoices (3:23)The storyteller describes the full coronation of H�kon as recognized by The Pope, and Norway's rejoicing, and H�kon's successes. There is some joyous music between narrative sections in a quick 6-8. Fun track!Track 11 - Frost Upon the Longships (4:38)Now that H�kon has cemented his position as King, he led Norway to become the most powerful nation in the Northern Seas. The refrains of the song are sung with only H�kon and the male members of the chorus, giving a very masculine sound. The tempo is moderately slow. There are big power chords and heavy drumming along with the orchestrations.Track 12 - Storms and Wrecks (3:51)This one describes the conflict over certain islands that broke out with rival Scotland. Mid-tempo, with some flute-like interludes. This one features Gemma Ashley's beautiful voice as Solveig. Wonderful performance!Track 13 - The King in the Mist (4:52)This is a mid-tempo bittersweet ballad, based on acoustic guitar, with H�kon describing his final days in the Orkney Islands during the Scottish Expedition. "Raise up the King in the mist, I'm ready to go home?"Track 14 - The Winter ThroneAfter the opening from the Storyteller, this one goes into a riff that sounds like a Symphonic Power Metal song. The chorus performs in Norse. It closes out the story harkening us to always remember the great reign of H�kon H�konarson!Bonus CD [Note- I have no real information about these tracks as to how they fit into the saga.]:Track 1 - We Are the Storm and The Iron (6:05)This seems to be an alternate version of "The Sword and the Fire". The lyrics are a bit different. The refrains are in English as opposed to Norse. Track 2 - Back to Varteig (4:40)One of the ladies is speaking in Norse, as opposed to The Storyteller with dramatic music accompanying. She then sings what appears to be a lullaby, in English. The other female leads join in harmony.Track 3 - Strings and Necks (3:20)I think the title refers to the guitar solo in this track. Well actually both electric and acoustic guitar solos. An outstanding (almost) instrumental track that lets the guitarists stretch out and be featured. There is a bit of a chant from one of the ladies near the end of the track. Track 4 - Crowns Across Time (4:31)This seems to be an alternate version of "The Puppet Crown". This one seems to be a little more basic in the arrangement/production; more stripped down.Track 5 - In the Mist (4:51)Once again, one of the ladies is speaking in Norse at the beginning. After that it is an alternate version of "The King in the Mist" in a more basic form, but it's sung from the perspective of one of the female characters. It seems that Clive changed his mind in regards to the point of view on some parts of the story. She speaks in Norse again at the end of the track.Track 6 - The First Prince (4:00)This is an alternate version of "The Hidden Prince" without The Storyteller at the beginning. Also a more stripped down version. I am thinking that many of these are demos/early versions. The harmonies are wonderful, only accompanied by a drumbeat at one point.Track 7 - Ritual of Faith Ceremonial Mix (3:36)No Storyteller at the beginning. There is only a basic drum accompaniment, so the vocals really pop out! The vocals are absolutely pristine!Track 8 - More Wreckage (3:50)It begins in Norse with one of the ladies speaking, as some of the others have. An alternate version of "Storms and Wrecks".Track 9 - Purely Instrumental Flight (3:33)Despite the title, I hear some "throat singing" as this begins. There are gothic choir sounds as well. This is the backing track from "Flight of the Birkebeiners" without the lead vocals. It's an impressive piece of music either way!Track 10 - Puppet Frets (4:32)The guitarists get the spotlight on this version of "The Puppet Crown".Track 11 - Frost Upon the Longships - Backing Track (4:01)The title tells you all you need to know!Track 12 - The Narration Fireside Mix (8:13)This is all of the "Storyteller" narration combined into one track. It recapitulates the opening stanza at the end, to give it a sense of completion.OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:This is begging to be staged! If anyone is capable of doing that, it is certainly Clive Nolan! With his experience in leading Caamora Theatre Company, I would not be surprised if that is already the plan. This is grand musical storytelling at its finest! The arrangements, performances, playing, singing and production are all flawless! If you are a fan of "Jeff Wayne's Musical Version of The War of the Worlds", then this is right up your alley! Three years ago, in September of 2023, I gave that album a 4 out of 5 Stars (80%). I like this one even better than that, but it is not quite one of my absolute favorites of 2026. Don't get me wrong, this is a production on an absolutely epic scale and it is achieved magnificently! Many kudos to Clive Nolan for what he and his massive cast of collaborators have accomplished here! However, I am giving it a near perfect 4.75 out of 5 (95%) as there are a few albums out there that appeal to my tastes a little more in 2026. I am certain that some will unabashedly give it a perfect score, and I certainly wouldn't fault them for it! Again, as I keep saying, 2026 has been an amazing year and prog, and almost on a daily basis, I get offered even more potentially amazing albums to review. This album certainly reinforces my assertion that 2026 will go down as one of the most amazing years in the modern prog era.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以挪威国王Håkon Håkonsson的历史故事为概念框架，呈现为一套大型叙事工程：双碟共约两小时，由作曲家兼键盘手Clive Nolan主导编曲、编程与管弦乐编排，邀请多位乐手和38人合唱团参与录制。制作上以键盘、鼓、吉他与管乐为核心配器，辅以剧情化的角色演唱。专辑本身属于新前卫摇滚范畴，在结构上偏向宏大叙事与古典管弦配器的融合，但整体手法更接近传统概念专辑的剧作式表达。乐评详细介绍了专辑背景、参与者名单与历史背景，但正文对音乐的实质分析尚未展开，文本更像项目介绍而非深入的听觉评价。

items.body: A Rammstein producer, a string section and a major label: Covenant made their fifth album under different conditions from the four before it. Ka2 Music, a division of Sony Music, released “Northern Light” in Europe on 30 September 2002, and Metropolis Records followed in the United States on 8 October 2002. The Swedish futurepop trio from Helsingborg had spent its previous albums on the independents Memento Materia, Off Beat and Dependent Records. The album turns 24 this year. Jacob Hellner, who had produced Rammstein’s first three albums, produced “Northern Light” after pre-production by the band. Stefan Glaumann mixed “Call the Ships to Port”, “Bullet”, “Invisible & Silent” and “Prometheus”, Ulf Kruckenberg mixed the other seven tracks, and Björn Engelmann mastered. Axwell added programming, Ricard Nettermalm played live drums and Lizzie Zachrisson sang backing vocals on “Bullet”, “Scared” and “Atlas”. The Stockholm Session Orchestra, arranged and conducted by Joakim Milder, played the strings on “Invisible & Silent”, and Ulf Ivarsson played bass on “Atlas”. Joakim Montelius wrote the lyrics for seven tracks and Eskil Simonsson for five. “Rising Sun” carries a co-writing credit for American techno producer Steve Stoll and uses elements of his tracks “Reciproheat” and “Falling Down”. The eleven tracks run 58 minutes and 39 seconds: “Monochrome”, “Call the Ships to Port”, “Bullet”, “Invisible & Silent”, “Prometheus”, “We Stand Alone”, “Rising Sun”, “Winter Comes”, “We Want Revolution”, “Scared” and “Atlas”. Ka2 issued the album as a standard CD, a limited digipak CD and a numbered gatefold double vinyl of 1,000 copies. The vinyl added four tracks not on the CD: club versions of “Bullet” and “Call the Ships to Port”, “Bullet (Funky Indian)” and “Don’t Go”. The Sony CDs carried copy protection and a label reading “Auf PC/Mac nicht abspielbar”, and early copies came with a sticker listing the “Northern Light” tour dates. Metropolis pressed its US edition as an HDCD. Two singles bracketed the release. “Call the Ships to Port” came out on 12 August 2002 as a CD maxi with remixes by Oliver Klitzing, Christian Morgenstern, Kaylab and Thomas P. Heckmann, and reached number 93 on the German singles chart. “Bullet” followed on 9 December 2002 with an Ellen Allien “Flow Mix”, a Le Dust Sucker mix and the otherwise unreleased “Atom Heart”. A “Bullet” DVD with the video and making-of footage appeared in January 2003. About Covenant Eskil Simonsson, Joakim Montelius and Clas Nachmanson, three school friends from Helsingborg in southern Sweden, started making music together in 1986 after seeing Front 242’s first Scandinavian show, and took the name Covenant in 1988. They built a studio in Nachmanson’s bedroom while studying in Lund. Their first released track, “The Replicant”, appeared on a Memento Materia compilation in 1992, and the label issued the debut album “Dreams of a Cryotank” in December 1994. Off Beat signed the trio in 1995 after a German festival appearance. “Sequencer” followed in May 1996, with the “Stalker” single and a tour alongside Haujobb and Steril later that year. San Francisco label 21st Circuitry handled the United States, where the “Theremin” EP appeared in 1997. “Europa” came out in April 1998. When Off Beat closed in 1999, Covenant moved to the newly formed Dependent Records in Germany and SubSpace Communications in Sweden, while Metropolis Records took over the American catalogue. “United States of Mind” appeared in February 2000, with the “Der Leiermann” single, and the live album “Synergy” followed in November 2000. “Northern Light” moved the band to Sony’s Ka2 division in 2002. By then Montelius lived in Barcelona and Simonsson in Berlin, with Nachmanson still in Helsingborg. “Skyshaper” arrived in March 2006, and in March 2007 the band announced that Nachmanson would no longer tour, with Daniel Myer of Haujobb taking his place on stage. The tour film “In Transit” came out on DVD in October 2007 and confirmed Nachmanson’s departure. “Modern Ruin” followed in January 2011, the first album with Myer as a full member, and Daniel Jonasson joined the live line-up that year. Andreas Catjar joined in 2013 on keyboards and guitar, playing on “Leaving Babylon” in September 2013 and on “The Blinding Dark”, released on 4 November 2016 after the “Sound Mirrors” single. Montelius told Side-Line at the time that the line-up had grown to five, and that “Covenant’s basic principle is to always evolve: change is the only constant.” The band handed out the “Fieldworks: Exkursion” EP on its German tour in February 2019 and released a cover of Yazoo’s “Winter Kills” in December 2020. Andreas Catjar-Danielsson died on 29 July 2024 after a long illness, and the charity “Andreas EP”, recorded with Simonsson, came out on Dependent Records on 17 October 2025. Twenty-four years after Ka2 pressed it, “Northern Light” remains the album that brought “Call the Ships to Port” and “Bullet” into the Covenant catalogue.
items._cn_summary: 本文为Covenant第五张专辑《Northern Light》发行24周年的信息整理，属于事实性资料汇编而非乐评。文章记录了专辑的制作团队配置——Rammstein前三张专辑的制作人Jacob Hellner担纲制作，弦乐部分由斯德哥尔摩Session Orchestra录制，并邀请了多位客座乐手参与编程、鼓和伴唱。同时列出全部十一首曲目、多种发行格式、CD/Vinyl附加曲目、两支单曲的混音阵容及德国单曲榜成绩等信息。该文对音乐本身的艺术特征、声音设计、创作思路缺乏任何分析与评论，仅以制作和发行信息为主，未触及音乐风格的突破性或实验性表达。

items.body: The Mission’s tenth studio album, “Another Fall from Grace,” turns 10 this year. The English gothic rock band released the record on 30 September 2016 through Eyes Wide Shut Recordings. Wayne Hussey has described the album as a link between The Sisters of Mercy’s “First and Last and Always” and The Mission’s own debut, “God’s Own Medicine,” citing his return to 12-string guitar as part of that connection. “Another Fall from Grace” runs just over an hour across twelve tracks and was produced by Wayne Hussey and Tim Palmer, with Palmer also mixing at ’62 Studios in Austin, Texas, and mastering by James Bacon. All songs were written by Hussey, except “Another Fall From Grace,” “Can’t See the Ocean for the Rain” and “Valaam,” co-written with Simon Hinkler. The album features a run of guest vocalists: Julianne Regan on the title track and closer “Phantom Pain,” Ville Valo of HIM on “Met-Amor-Phosis,” Gary Numan on “Within the Deepest Darkness (Fearful),” Evi Vine on “Can’t See the Ocean for the Rain” and “Never’s Longer Than Forever,” and Martin Gore of Depeche Mode on backing vocals for “Only You & You Alone.” Duke Garwood contributes alto clarinet and saxophone on “Phantom Pain.” The tracklist runs “Another Fall From Grace,” “Met-Amor-Phosis,” “Within the Deepest Darkness (Fearful),” “Blood on the Road,” “Can’t See the Ocean for the Rain,” “Tyranny of Secrets,” “Never’s Longer Than Forever,” “Bullets & Bayonets,” “Valaam,” “Jade,” “Only You & You Alone” and “Phantom Pain.” The album peaked at number 38 on the UK Albums Chart, number 2 on the UK Rock & Metal Albums Chart and number 49 in Germany. A deluxe edition followed in 2017 under the title “The Complete Another Fall From Grace,” adding a bonus disc and DVD. About The Mission The Mission formed in Leeds, England, in 1986 after Wayne Hussey and Craig Adams left The Sisters of Mercy. The pair recruited guitarist Simon Hinkler and drummer Mick Brown, initially performing as The Sisterhood before settling on The Mission. The band signed to Mercury/Phonogram’s Chapter 22 offshoot and released its debut single, “Serpent’s Kiss,” in 1986, followed by the debut album “God’s Own Medicine” in 1986, which reached the UK top ten. Through the late 1980s and 1990s, The Mission released a run of albums including “Children” (1988), “Carved in Sand” (1990), “Masque” (1992) and “Neverland” (1995), with several lineup changes affecting the rhythm section while Hussey remained the constant frontman. The band went on hiatus multiple times before reconvening for later studio work, including “God Is a Bullet” (2007), “The Brightest Light” (2013) and “Another Fall from Grace” in 2016, the latter recorded with Craig Adams back on bass and Mike Kelly on drums alongside Hussey and Hinkler. “Another Fall from Grace” brought together guest contributions from Gary Numan, Martin Gore, Ville Valo and Julianne Regan, produced by Tim Palmer and released through Eyes Wide Shut Recordings. Ten years on, the album stands as one of the band’s most complete studio statements of its post-2000s period.
items._cn_summary: 本文为The Mission第十张录音室专辑《Another Fall from Grace》十周年的回顾性资讯，由Side-Line发布。文章以事实陈述为主：介绍专辑于2016年9月30日由Eyes Wide Shut Recordings发行，由Wayne Hussey与Tim Palmer联合制作，长度超过一小时共12首曲目，Hussey称之为回归12弦吉他、连接Sisters of Mercy首作与乐队自身处女作风格的纽带。文章罗列了多位客串音乐人名单、曲目顺序及英德排行榜成绩，并附有2017年推出的豪华版信息。文章最后简述乐队1986年于利兹成立的历史背景、成员沿革与主要专辑年表。全文未涉及实际音乐分析或听觉评价，属于信息整理性质的纪念性报道，缺乏评论深度与艺术性洞察。

items.body: With autumn extending its chilly tendrils and release season in full swing, I found myself in the welcome but somewhat overwhelming company of three album promo’s clamoring for review. Fortunately we have a perfect if seldom used format for this that may be dredged up from the blog’s murky depths when needed. Here we go...Brymir – What We Leave BehindIf you know Brymir, you know what they do. That may be one of my least inspired opening lines ever, but I stand by it. These Finnish purveyors of melodic death metal embellish the well-established style of Finnish melodeath with sweeping orchestral arrangements, mostly resulting in a predictable but no less exhilarating couple of absolute banging tracks on an album generally overshadowed by other acts. What We Leave Behind might claim to be Brymir's “most sinister album yet”, according to the promo, but I’m still getting my saccharine fix of high-octane full-blast-melody bangers and that’s what I want. I think Brymir and/or their label are largely aware of this, since they usually manage to drop these as advance singles. For your periodic fix of indelible, vanquishing albums akin to “Wings of Fire” and “Voices in the Sky”, look no further than “Tempestbound”, and especially the title track.For those curious as to what a darker Brymir might entail, I’ve found this plan largely successful. “True Darkness” and “Buried Legion” offer a more aggressive take on their established formula, and “The Roaring King” and “Broken Dawn” achieve varying success with a slower approach. While an Aether Realm like grandiosity permeates the tracks, they can be a tad indulgent and fatiguing towards the end of an album that already carries the weight of much bombast. While hilarious, unexpected, and surprisingly apt for their style, the closing cover of Scooter's “How Much is the Fish” (you’ll know it when you hear the melody) is a bit of a contradictory choice for an album that’s supposed to show their serious side. That being said, if you liked their previous album’s I’d bet you’ll like this one too. More Brymir being Brymir is hardly a bad thing, and I’m sure I’ll wake up in a few months with one of their earworms randomly crawling around in my brain.  What We Leave Behind by Brymir What We Leave Behind by Brymir Firtan – HeliosI’ve been following now-German sextet Firtan with intermittently bated breath since my first encounter with 2018s Okeanos. Firtan’s music is firmly rooted in icy black metal, but find sit’s most arresting foothold when the band’s progressive and symphonic leanings join the furious fray. While cuts like “Seegang” and “Uferlos” (2018), “Amor Fati’and “Peraht” (2022) and “Hrenga” (2024) showed glimpses of a ravenous yet poised and grandiose talent on each of their past three albums, Firtan have yet to write an album that sweeps me away as a whole. On their previous three releases, many excellent tracks or movements felt like sweeping vista’s being crammed into the corners of an overcrowded tableau. Arresting and immediately memorable, but ultimately groaning under the weight of overindulgence or less memorable surrounding compositions. Helios, while by no means a stark departure from their established sound, does show Firtan taking steps towards greater consistency and a more measured style of blackened metal. Abandoning some of the slavering hunger and much of the speedy outbursts present on previous albums, they opt for a more doom and death metal inspired soundscape, drawing parallels to particularly Schammasch. While this approach works well to keep songs more focused, it also exposes their sometimes unnecessary length,and makes the album sag under an entirely different but no less noticeable weight at times. Slowing down does allow both acoustic elements  and some of the more death/doom oriented riffing to shine. “Kalika’s Tongue”, “Solis Currus”, “Helios” and “The Hierophant” show the shining promise in Firtan’s new approach, and if they reintroduce some of the wilder aspects from earlier releases and intertwine them with the patience and focus on display on Helios, their next release may very well live up to the expectations that I’ve been quietly carrying around since I first heard that inimitable riff of “Seegang”all those years ago. Helios by Firtan Temic – CeibaIt’s been a while since I’ve written about an album so ingrained in heavy, modern prog (metal) as this one. Those roots come as no surprise when reading of the associated pedigree that comes with this relatively young and unheralded super-group. Featuring (ex or current) members of Devin Townsend, Mike Portnoy’s Shattered Fortress, the Neal Morse Band, Haken, Shining (Nor) and Maraton is a serious endorsement. Prog super-groups, however, are also notoriously prone to writing indulgent if not masturbatory escapades of soulless technicality. Fortunately, Temic manage to avoid this latter pitfall. While the occasional keyboard or guitar solo can test my patience, the album (at least for a prog metal album) is generally well paced and only features one 10-minute-plus song. In terms of influence, it’s mainly (older) Haken that springs to mind, as well as Leprous, Votum, Kingcrow and perhaps Caligula’s Horse. Somewhat ironically, the album’s less than polished vocal delivery might afford it most of its more obvious unique character. Had those rougher, accented edges not been present, I might have given up on the album before reaching its halfway point. That’s not to say it's bad by any means, I’ve just heard too many permutations of this particular style of prog to be easily impressed. Sticking around for the latter half of the album proves more interesting, with longer compositions less focused on generic heavy prog riffs and more of the charming melodicism and sweeping climaxes that elevate Temic above the sum of its well worn parts. “Casting Stone” and “See Myself” get the ball rolling, and momentum carries the album through to “Alone” and obligatory long and ambitious closer “As Long As We Last”, which drifts towards Southern Empire’s criminally underrated Civilisation in tone and mood (if not in song length). Ceiba is a good and occasionally great progressive metal album, just don’t expect to be blown away if you’re familiar with the style.  Ceiba by TEMIC

items.excerpt: 2026.09.30 9月29日、サントリーホール ブルーローズにて、第57回サントリー音楽賞を受賞した佐藤俊介（ヴァイオリン／指揮）と、第25回佐治敬三賞を受賞した「日野浩志郎新作音楽公演『Chronograffiti』」の贈賞式が行なわれた。 サントリー音楽賞は1969年の創設以来、毎年、その前年度においてわが国の洋楽文化の発展にもっとも顕著な功績のあった個人または団体を顕彰し、贈呈している。賞金は700万円。 贈賞理由には、「分断に歪み、混迷を深めるいまの時代において、芸術家にしかできないことをアクチュアルに示し続けている。楽しむだけではなく、思考を突き動かすためにこそ、音楽を。そうした佐藤のビジョンを照らし、クラシック音楽の未来の一翼を担うひとりとして、今後の歩みへの期待を示すもの」ということがあげられている。 ビーバー《ロザリオのソナタ》よりパッサカリアを演奏して喝采を浴びた後、贈賞式でスピーチを行なう佐藤俊介。 ヴァイオリニストであり、指揮者、室内楽奏者である佐藤俊介は、世界各地のピリオド楽器アンサンブルやシンフォニック・オーケストラを指揮し、ソリストとしても出演。2013
items.body: 2026.09.30 9月29日、サントリーホール ブルーローズにて、第57回サントリー音楽賞を受賞した佐藤俊介（ヴァイオリン／指揮）と、第25回佐治敬三賞を受賞した「日野浩志郎新作音楽公演『Chronograffiti』」の贈賞式が行なわれた。 サントリー音楽賞は1969年の創設以来、毎年、その前年度においてわが国の洋楽文化の発展にもっとも顕著な功績のあった個人または団体を顕彰し、贈呈している。賞金は700万円。 贈賞理由には、「分断に歪み、混迷を深めるいまの時代において、芸術家にしかできないことをアクチュアルに示し続けている。楽しむだけではなく、思考を突き動かすためにこそ、音楽を。そうした佐藤のビジョンを照らし、クラシック音楽の未来の一翼を担うひとりとして、今後の歩みへの期待を示すもの」ということがあげられている。 ビーバー《ロザリオのソナタ》よりパッサカリアを演奏して喝采を浴びた後、贈賞式でスピーチを行なう佐藤俊介。 ヴァイオリニストであり、指揮者、室内楽奏者である佐藤俊介は、世界各地のピリオド楽器アンサンブルやシンフォニック・オーケストラを指揮し、ソリストとしても出演。2013～23年オランダ・バッハ協会のコンサートマスターを、18年からは音楽監督を兼務し、録音したJ.S.バッハのカンタータや器楽作品の数々は、同協会のYouTubeで見ることができる。2011年からはコンチェルト・ケルンのソリスト、指揮者、コンサートマスターを務め、2013年からアムステルダム音楽院の教授としてヒストリカル・ヴァイオリンを教えている 贈賞式に登壇した佐藤は、「たいへん光栄であると同時に、身の引き締まる思い。ブルーローズは特別な思い入れがある場所で、26年前の2000年、当時16歳だった私は日本で初めてのコンサートを行なうことになり、その会場の1つがここだった。 4歳から19歳までずっとアメリカに住んでいて、当時は日本語の敬語がうまく使えず、アンコールの曲名を伝えるのに、お客様に向かってタメ口で話してしまった（笑）。そんなデビュー当時のとんちんかんな私でさえ、何かのスタート地点に立っているという意識はあったが、まさか26年後にサントリー音楽賞の受賞者として、再びこの同じステージに上がらせていただくとは思っていなかった。 この26年間、多くの方に出会い、ご指導いただき、私の未熟さや失敗を寛容に受け入れてくださり、私の音楽家としての価値を信じてくださった。困難や迷いに遭遇した時もあったが、これらの方々一人ひとりのおかげで、今の自分がここにいることを考えると、今回の賞を受賞したのは自分だけではないということを痛感する。 本日の贈賞式も、今の私にとって新たなスタート地点であるような気がする。これからどんな経験をし、どんな出会いが待っているか、楽しみでならない。これまで私を導いてくださった先生方、共演してくださった音楽家の皆様、演奏の場を作り支えてくださった皆様、そして何より演奏会場で音楽を共にしてくださった聴衆の皆様に、心より感謝申し上げる」と述べた。 最新アルバム『BEE1H0VEN~ベートーヴェン：ヴァイオリン・ソナタ全集』が新レコード・アカデミー賞第1回大賞に輝き、2027年4月からは、東京交響楽団のクリエイティブ・パートナーを3年間務めることになった佐藤。今年5月からは、自身が創設したロマン派以降の音楽を主な対象とする古楽オーケストラ「Past Forward Ensemble」の演奏活動もスタートした。 「強い信念で周囲の音楽家を巻き込みながら、卓越した行動力で新しい音楽の潮流を作っていく。日本の次世代を担う音楽家たちに大きな影響を与え、これからますます存在感を発揮していく」（サントリー音楽財団代表理事 堤剛氏）と讃えられる佐藤が、今後ヴァイオリニストとして、指揮者として、ますます多く日本の聴衆の前に姿を現してくれることを願ってやまない。
items._cn_summary: 本文为第57回サントリー音楽賞贈賞式の報道記事であり、受賞者であるヴァイオリニスト兼指揮者の佐藤俊介の経歴と授賞理由、受賞スピーチの内容を紹介する。佐藤はピリオド楽器アンサンブルのコンサートマスターや指揮者として国際的に活動し、J.S.バッハの録音や古楽オーケストラ「Past Forward Ensemble」の創設など、ヒストリカル・インフォームド・パフォーマンスの分野で活躍している。記事では即興や現代作曲への言及は乏しく、バッハやベートーヴェンといった古典レパートリーの演奏が中心。実験的手法やジャンル横断的な試みの記述はほぼ見当たらず、受賞イベントの事実関係と本人の謝辞が主軸となっている。

items.excerpt: 今年8月から渋谷のユーロスペースで始まり、現在は全国各地にその上映場所を移している「パフォーマンス・アート：身体と空間をめぐる映画祭」。合計4プログラム5作品のドキュメンタリーからなる特集上映ですが、東京在住の筆者はこの夏、予定の隙間を見つけては劇場に足を運び、なんとか全作コンプリート（それを可能にしてくれた長期間のプログラム編成に感謝）。そのいずれもが観に来てよかったとしみじみ思える作品たちでした。 夏の日差しがもはや懐かしい［筆者撮影］ 折角なら全作観ようと思えるこの「映画祭」のサイズ感も心地良く、作品同士の連関にはっとするだけでなく、そこで観たものが別の場所や次の季節でまた別のものに出会わせてくれる、というおまけのような循環も。例えばプログラムDの『ナム・ジュン・パイク 月は最古のTV』（アマンダ・キム監督、2023）を観た後にワタリウム美術館の「没後20年 ナムジュン・パイク｜じゅげむ展」（11月23日まで）を観ると、彼の作品のなかの音楽やパフォーマンスの部分に自然とフォーカスするようになったりと、また体験が変わります。あるいはピナ・バウシュとヴッパタール舞踊団の欧州ツアーを追

items.body: Sometimes, the band is the standout performance. What’s up, everyone! Welcome back to yet another installment of the J-Music Exchange/Rate! Your monthly source of Japanese music album reviews brought to you by yours truly and my good friend and fellow Japanese music fan Al from Omunibasu. If you’ve been rocking with us for a while now, then you already know the deal, but if this is your first time here and you’re not entirely sure what the Exchange/Rate is all about, please give the following primer a quick readーThe Exchange/Rate is a tandem album review series conducted every month by yours truly alongside my good friend and fellow Japanese music fan Al (from Omunibasu). Each month we decide on a specific theme with which our reviews would revolve around. We then pick out albums from our respective libraries which we think best coincides with that theme. We will then give the album we chose to the other person and vice versa (exchange), after which we then listen to and subsequently review the album we were given (rate). This project has not only allowed us to explore music beyond our libraries, but it provides an opportunity for us to see our favorite albums from a different point of view. It is our hope that this series is able to do the same for you and that you either find a new artist to try out and/or we offer you a fresh take on one of *your* favorite albums Al and I take turns deciding on a theme for our reviews every month, and for September we’re handing the reins back over to him. And I gotta say, I thought he came up with a pretty interesting one this time around, as we’ll be talking about albums that we feel exemplify an excellent group effort. Now, what exactly do we mean by that? Well, I don’t necessarily think it’s as simple as picking out an album where everyone involved is just really good at what they do. Rather, we’re looking at releases where you can genuinely feel the importance of everyone’s contributions to the finished work. Where the drums, bass, guitars, vocals, keys, production, or whatever else might be involved all feel integral to what makes the album what it is, and where taking any one of those elements away would leave you with something noticeably different. Of course, how that group effort manifests can vary quite a bit from one album to another, which is also what makes this such a fun theme to explore. For my pick, I went ahead and gave Al Fooocus by Aooo, a release that I think demonstrates the concept particularly well with how each of its members gets an opportunity to bring their own musical identity into the fold while still working together as one cohesive unit. You can check out what Al thought of that over at the Omunibasu Substack! Al, meanwhile, decided to send me Mani Mani by CRCK/LCKS, an album made by a group of musicians who, as we’re about to find out, have quite the collective pedigree between them. And perhaps more importantly for today’s discussion, they might just have a thing or two to teach us about what happens when you put that much individual talent in the same room. Let’s get into it! ーー CRCK/LCKS (クラックラックス) is a five-piece Japanese band formed in 2015, consisting of vocalist/keyboardist Oda Tomomi, saxophonist and multi-instrumentalist Konishi Ryo, guitarist Inoue Mei, bassist Ochi Shunsuke, and drummer Ishikawa Shun. Comprised of musicians with backgrounds predominantly rooted in jazz, the group brings together their respective expertise to create a style that freely moves between jazz, pop, R&B, and other contemporary influences, with an emphasis on intricate ensemble work and experimentation. ＜Ｍａｎｉ Ｍａｎｉ (まにまに)＞(＊Spotify link to the full album) CDJapan Affiliate Link(s):Mani Mani / CRCK/LCKS ＜T ｒａｃｋｌｉｓｔ＞ ０１・あらわらわ/arawarawa０２・レンタル神様/rental kamisama０３・真空パック/shinkuu pack０４・Psycho Sky０５・T.I.C.０６・沖に出たら/oki ni detara０７・枝と嵐/eda to arashi０８・バラライカ/balalaika０９・つまらない毎日/tsumaranai mainichi１０・Tiny Mirror１１・7月27日１２・You say goodbye１３・manimani Ａｌ：Ever since I first discovered CRCK/LCKS a few years ago, I’ve always found them to be a pretty fascinating band. It’s possible that I didn’t fully grasp what they were all about at first, but their two Temporary albums were ones I’d always come back to randomly, just because of how avant-garde the songs were and their overall irregular take on pop music. One moment you could be hearing a groovy cacophony of guitar, bass, and even the saxophone going wild, and another moment can have you getting lost in an ethereal soundscape. They may be a group that I have an on-and-off listening relationship with, but their ability to come up with this nutty stuff never fails to catch my attention. And I do feel like that’s why I came to enjoy their most recent album, Manimani, a lot. I’ll admit that the thought process for this month’s theme was based on how much more perceptive I’ve become when I listen to music, with me often trying to mentally separate the instrumental and/or vocal performances in a song, in order to really appreciate everyone’s efforts individually (and thus, understanding how well it all gels together). And with a band like CRCK/LCKS, who seem to display so many different elements in their music, it’s hard not to take interest in the mesmerizing or pleasant oddities they’ve been known for. Especially considering how varied the song selection is on Manimani, as the band showcases a more rambunctious side in the opener’s ending sequence (“arawarawa”), the unbelievably calming jazzy nature of “edatoarashi”, or how the bouncy and weirdly hyper traits in song like “bararaika” made it a standout song during my initial go-through with the album… it’s a record that feels very familiar if you’re an existing fan of the band, yet their efforts still feel super fresh with how surprisingly varied it is, style-wise. Another reason why I might’ve picked this one was because it’s described to be a cool celebration of CRCK/LCKS’ existence as a group, and every single member is featured on its songwriting credits. And after finding that out, it made it clear how much of a collective effort this album was, with everyone being able to chip in with their own ideas. And honestly, it resulted in an even more of an enjoyable experience. ーー Now, I actually thought about doing this one a little bit differently than I normally do for Exchange/Rate album reviews. If you’re a longtime follower of this series and are thus quite familiar with how I structure my end of the reviews, you’ll know that I typically pick out, at minimum, four songs from the album to talk about. These aren’t necessarily always my four favorite tracks either. More often than not, I use them to formulate a framework for how I want to approach the record as a whole; what I find good or intriguing about it, what I think the artist is trying to accomplish, and ultimately what kind of music listening experience I believe the album has to offer. In spending some time with CRCK/LCKS’ Mani Mani, however, I very quickly realized that I can’t really go about doing that here. Or, perhaps more accurately, I don’t think I should. Part of my reasoning for that is ultimately going to be at the heart of my overall thoughts on the album, but I think a good place to start this discussion is by first looking at the individual parts that make up CRCK/LCKS. Because if we’re going to talk about Mani Mani, I think we first have to talk about the people who made it. The band is led by multi-instrumentalist and Berklee College of Music graduate Konishi Ryo, known primarily within Japanese jazz circles for his work on the saxophone. Joining him on keys and vocals is classically trained Oda Tomomi, with jazz guitarist Inoue Mei on guitar, Ochi Shunsuke on bass, and Tokyo University of the Arts graduate and credentialed percussionist Ishikawa Shun behind the drums. For your everyday overseas Japanese music fan, I don’t necessarily expect all of those names to immediately jump off the page. For those more entrenched in the Japanese jazz scene in particular, however, seeing these five musicians come together in service of one collaborative project might read as something closer to a supergroup. Across the five members are numerous accolades and accomplishments within the Japanese music world, with each having established themselves through their own work and collaborations with renowned musicians both within and outside of Japan. All of which is to say that nobody in CRCK/LCKS necessarily needs the band to prove what they’re capable of individually. Everyone involved is already exceptionally accomplished at what they do. Which, naturally, begs a much more interesting question. What happens when you put all five of them together? That’s ultimately where my interest in Mani Mani lies. With this much individual talent packed into one group, it would be incredibly easy to approach the album by pulling everything apart and pointing toward what each member contributes. But I also think doing so would miss what makes CRCK/LCKS so fascinating in the first place. The question I’m more interested in asking isn’t what each of these five musicians can do individually. It’s whether what they create together amounts to something greater than the sum of its parts. Given how skilled everyone in CRCK/LCKS is with their respective instruments, I think it would be perfectly natural to assume that there’d eventually be some sense of one member overpowering another. Put five musicians of this caliber together and surely someone is gonna end up taking over the room, right? Except, as you’ll hear even from the opening stretch with Arawarawa, and subsequently thereafter with songs like Rental kamisama and Shinkuu pack, that never really happens. Instead, there’s this remarkable cohesion to the way CRCK/LCKS perform together where nobody sounds as though they need to tone down their own musicality simply to accommodate the other virtuosos playing alongside them. Everyone is still very clearly doing what they do best, only somehow without any of it coming at the expense of somebody else. You can still hear and appreciate Ishikawa Shun’s impeccable drum work without it ever distracting from Oda Tomomi’s lovely singing. Likewise, Konishi Ryo can bring his saxophone into the arrangement without completely stealing the spotlight away from Inoue Mei and Ochi Shunsuke on guitar and bass respectively. Nobody necessarily has to retreat into the background for somebody else to shine. And I think that’s an important distinction to make when talking about Mani Mani. The impressive thing isn’t simply that five extremely talented musicians are able to play well together. You’d probably expect that much given everyone’s credentials. It’s that they can seemingly play to the full extent of their abilities at the same time and still sound like a band rather than five individually impressive performances happening on top of one another. Part of me wants to simply chalk that up to the members being incredibly compatible with one another. At the very least, you don’t get the impression listening to Mani Mani that anyone feels the need to constantly prove themselves or overshadow everybody else in the room. But I do want to pose another possibility as to why CRCK/LCKS work so well together, and that’s the fact that all five of them come from jazz backgrounds. Obviously, there’s already going to be some preexisting overlap there. Having five musicians who operate within the same general musical space naturally gives them a shared foundation to work from. What I’m more interested in, however, is jazz itself and how the characteristics of the genre might have helped provide CRCK/LCKS with that unifying thread. Jazz is, by nature, a remarkably loose and unrestricted style of music. One of its most defining characteristics is improvisation, which inherently asks musicians to be responsive not only to what they’re playing, but also to what’s happening around them at any given moment. A performance can shift depending on what somebody else decides to do, leaving everyone involved to react and find their place within it. There’s a certain volatility to jazz in that regard, but I also think that’s precisely what makes it so conducive to having this many different elements operating at once. And perhaps that’s part of why CRCK/LCKS never feel overcrowded despite how much musicianship is constantly on display throughout Mani Mani. These aren’t simply five talented musicians who happen to be playing alongside one another. They’re five musicians coming from a musical tradition that, at its core, places a tremendous amount of value on listening and responding to the people playing alongside you. So when Ishikawa changes something on the drums, or Konishi comes through with the saxophone, or Inoue and Ochi start working something between the guitar and bass, everyone else has the musical vocabulary to respond accordingly. Their individual contributions don’t have to be planned around as obstacles; they become opportunities for everybody else to build upon. In that sense, jazz isn’t merely one of the styles that informs CRCK/LCKS’ music. It might very well be the reason all of these moving parts fit together as naturally as they do. In that regard, I do view Mani Mani as something closer to one big jazz jam session between the members of CRCK/LCKS more than anything else, and this is again largely why I decided not to approach this Exchange/Rate the way I normally would. Rather than viewing the album as a collection of individual songs and picking apart specific moments contained within them, I think Mani Mani works better as a showcase of what these five musicians are capable of creating together. It’s less about waiting for any one member to step forward and give you that big standout performance, and more about listening to how everyone continuously interacts with and plays off one another as the album moves along. Though there’s another side to that too, which is that there honestly aren’t that many singular moments throughout Mani Mani that I find myself wanting to isolate in the first place. And I don’t necessarily mean that as a criticism. If anything, part of what made it so difficult for me to pick out four songs to talk about is that the individual tracks themselves don’t really stand out that much over everything else on the album. There are certainly songs I enjoy more than others, with You say goodbye being the one clear exception for me as a song that I absolutely adore and would probably call my favorite track off Mani Mani simply for how beautiful it is. But beyond that, I rarely find myself listening to the album and thinking about one song being the song. Instead, CRCK/LCKS just… play. They create, they experiment, they respond to one another, and then they move on to the next idea. There’s a free-flowing quality to Mani Mani that makes the boundaries between those individual tracks feel considerably less important than the experience of hearing the band perform across the album as a whole. In that sense, listening to Mani Mani reminds me a lot of sitting down at a jazz bar and taking in a live set. You might walk away remembering a particular melody or moment that caught your ear, but that’s not necessarily why you enjoyed yourself. Sometimes the pleasure comes simply from sitting there and watching a group of incredibly capable musicians do their thing, seeing where the music takes them and appreciating how naturally they’re able to find one another along the way. That’s more or less how I find myself listening to Mani Mani. And perhaps that’s the best explanation I can give as to why, for once, I don’t really want to pull the album apart into four songs and tell you what makes each one work. The thing I find most interesting about Mani Mani isn’t any singular moment contained within it. It’s CRCK/LCKS themselves. ＜Ｗｈａｔ Ｉ ｔｈｉｎｋ ｏｆ Ｍａｎｉ Ｍａｎｉ ＞ So, after all of that, I suppose we’re left with the question that I posed at the very beginning: is CRCK/LCKS as a collective greater than the sum of its parts? Well… yes and no. If we’re looking at Mani Mani purely as a showcase of what happens when you put five incredibly accomplished musicians together and let them create, then I do think the answer is a resounding yes. There’s a level of musical understanding between everyone involved that allows each member to perform at an incredibly high level without ever making the album feel like a competition for your attention. Nobody gets lost, but nobody has to overpower everybody else either. Instead, their respective talents continually feed into one another, and I think the jazz background shared between them goes a long way toward explaining why that interaction feels as natural as it does. At the same time, I do think there’s another side to that equation when we start looking at Mani Mani specifically as an album. Going back to my comparison of listening to the record as being akin to sitting through a live set at a jazz bar, there are naturally opportunities for the mind to meander between songs. And I did find myself doing that here. There were a couple of times listening through Mani Mani where I noticed my attention starting to drift, only for the band to pick things back up instrumentally and pull me right back in again. Curiously enough, I almost wonder if that’s somewhat intentional. There are a lot of starts and stops throughout Mani Mani, along with these little interstitial tracks scattered between the more fully realized songs, to the point where it can sometimes feel like you’re supposed to lose track of exactly where you are in the album. One song ends, another idea comes in, the band pauses, something else begins, and eventually you look down and realize you’re three tracks further along than you thought you were. In most cases, I would probably consider that a knock against an album. After all, you’d generally want the songs themselves to leave enough of an impression that you can distinguish one from another. And as I mentioned earlier, outside of something like You say goodbye, there aren’t really many tracks on Mani Mani that I personally came away viewing as these huge individual landmarks. But I’m also not entirely convinced that Mani Mani wants to be experienced that way. The more time I spent with it, the less I found myself approaching the album as thirteen separate tracks and the more I started treating it as one continuous performance. Sometimes you’re completely locked in on what CRCK/LCKS are doing. Other times you let the music play while your mind wanders elsewhere. Then Ishikawa comes crashing back in on the drums, Konishi’s saxophone cuts through, Oda catches your ear with a vocal line, or Inoue and Ochi find another groove together and suddenly you’re paying attention again. And honestly, there’s something kind of pleasant about that. It makes Mani Mani less of an album where I’m constantly waiting for the next song I like to come on, and more of one where I simply enjoy spending time in the presence of the musicians playing it. The individual tracks become less important than the ebb and flow of the performance itself, which I think explains why trying to pick four of them apart for this review never quite felt right to me. So, is the whole greater than the sum of its parts? From a purely musical standpoint, absolutely. CRCK/LCKS are five tremendously accomplished musicians individually, but what makes Mani Mani interesting isn’t simply getting to hear all five of them demonstrate what they’re capable of. It’s hearing what each of them becomes in response to the other four. As an album, though, I think that same collective quality comes with a tradeoff. Mani Mani can be so free-flowing that its songs occasionally lose some of their individual identity along the way. But perhaps that’s also the point. Sometimes you don’t go to a jazz bar because you’re waiting to hear one particular song. Sometimes you go because the band is playing. ＜Ｍｙ Ｒａｔｉｎｇ＞４ ｏｕｔ ｏｆ ５ ＆ ８ ｏｕｔ ｏｆ １０ Mani Mani is, in a lot of ways, both memorable and unremarkable And I realize those two things sound like they shouldn’t be able to coexist, but I think that’s ultimately the best way I can summarize my experience with the album. Outside of something like You say goodbye, I don’t necessarily see myself walking away from Mani Mani remembering a bunch of individual songs or singular moments that completely blew me away. What I will remember, however, is the experience of listening to CRCK/LCKS play together. Because even during the moments where my attention started to drift, I don’t think there was ever a point where I questioned the quality of the musicianship on display. If anything, hearing five musicians this accomplished play alongside one another with seemingly very little interest in individually taking over the spotlight made me appreciate the collective that much more. Perhaps that’s also what makes Mani Mani such a fitting album for this month’s theme. When everyone involved is already this talented individually, it’d be easy for the appeal to simply become the novelty of hearing all of them on the same record. Instead, the most impressive thing about CRCK/LCKS is how quickly you stop thinking about any one member at all. ーー What are your guys’ thoughts on CRCK/LCKS’ Mani Mani? Let us know down in the comments! Likewise, what albums come to mind for you when you think of an excellent group effort? Whether it’s a band where every member feels integral to the music or simply a group of musicians who bring out the best in one another, we’d love to hear your picks! Lastly, before I let you guys go, don’t forget to check out Al’s review of Fooocus by Aooo over at the Omunibasu Substack if you haven’t yet! Happy Listening!
items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评来自一个每月双人互换专辑的主题企划，本期主题聚焦于'集体协作'的典范专辑。审查者挑选了 Aooo 的《Fooocus》与 Al 互评，而本文作者则收到了 CRCK/LCKS 的《Mani Mani》进行评论。文章用较大篇幅介绍了企划的背景与主题定义，强调集体协作不仅指成员各自技艺精湛，更在于每个人对专辑整体不可或缺的贡献。遗憾的是，正文在即将开始评价《Mani Mani》时便戛然而止，读者无法得知乐手背景、音乐风格细节、编曲特点或具体听后感受，因此对这张专辑本身几乎无法做出实质判断，仅能从标题推断这可能是一支注重集体即兴的日本器乐乐队作品。

items.body: Hitting its 40th anniversary, Julian Marszalek reckons that not only is Iggy Pop’s seventh solo record the most misunderstood of all of his LPs, but that it also happens to be David Bowie’s best album of the 80s Well, no one saw this one coming. Having spent the previous decade lauded as rock & roll’s most compelling survivor – an intoxicating mix of self-destruction, self-sabotage and musical innovation – Iggy Pop found himself, improbably, with a hit album on his hands. Not a reissue, not a compilation or a soundtrack, mind, but a bona fide triumph that would go on to be his most commercially successful album. And if that wasn’t enough, he then ram-raided – for the first and only... The post Real Wild Man: Iggy Pop’s Blah Blah Blah at 40 appeared first on The Quietus.
items._cn_summary: 本文纪念Iggy Pop第七张个人专辑发行四十周年，评论者认为这是他所有唱片中最被误解的一张，同时也是David Bowie在八十年代最好的专辑作品。Iggy Pop在前十年以摇滚乐幸存者的姿态获得赞誉，融合自我毁灭、自我破坏与音乐创新的矛盾特质。出人意料地，这张专辑成为他商业上最成功的作品，而非仅仅因再版、合辑或原声带而走红。文章未提供具体的音乐技术分析或曲目解读，更多聚焦于专辑的历史定位与文化语境。整体内容偏向回顾性叙事而非深入的音乐批评，且原文内容较短，信息有限。

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Reale Accademia Di Musica is a italien band from Rome, best known among us for its self-titled debut album released in 1972, an Italian progressive rock sound similar to that of PFM from the same era, though lacking the Milanese band's charisma. The rest of their discography, led by composer Adriano Monteduro under the acronym RAM, is of much less interest to us? until their 2018 revival spearheaded by Pericle Sponzilli, the band's original guitarist, who enlisted the talents of virtuoso keyboardist Fabio Liberatori (a prolific composer of Italian film scores) and Erika Savastani, a young singer with a powerful voice, to release *Angeli Mutanti* that year?an interesting, if not essential, fusion of modern Italian pop and flamboyant, timeless Italian progressive rock.*Lame Di Luce* is in the same vein, while at times drawing closer to the Italian neo-prog of the '90s (Leviathan, Mad Crayon?) as on the magnificent "Ascesa al Fuji," one of those gems that seems to smile at us and make life so sweet as it comes alive with vibrant colors. Fifty years later, the pastoral feel of the debut album is very much present on "Onde di Sabbia," and a few other echoes of the RPI masters charm us effortlessly (Le Orme on "Due Pietre Preziose Birmane" or Banco on the jazzy "Si Parler�"). This band excels at writing melodies that are out of the ordinary while remaining accessible to a wide audience, as heard on the irresistible "Lame di Luce," which seems to be to Italian song what the Moody Blues' music was to English prog: sophisticated pop without being ostentatious, capable of sounding harmonious even to the most delicate angels in heaven. The final quarter-hour of *Lame di Luce* may seem a bit weaker. "Una Ferita da Disinfettare" is a well-crafted symphonic prog track, but it will primarily catch our attention for a brief, unexpected quote from the famous guitar solo in "Firth of Fifth." "Ore Lente" could pass for a simple, dynamic song with a catchy chorus, and "Incontri" for a nostalgic Pink Floyd-style ballad that's a bit too slow?were it not for the cinematic influence of Fabio Liberatori, which enriches the mood and atmosphere of both tracks.Ultimately, the best moments carry the album and overshadow the few, quite excusable weaknesses, ensuring that our favorable opinion remains. *Lame di Luce* is a pleasant surprise and deserves our full attention. All it needs are a few more instrumental developments to make it an excellent modern RPI album worthy of its illustrious predecessors, among whom *Reale Accademia Di Musica* was counted in the early '70s.
items._genre: Italian progressive rock / neo-prog / symphonic prog
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是罗马乐队Reale Accademia Di Musica在2018年复出后的第二张作品，由原吉他手Pericle Sponzilli领衔，联手键盘手Fabio Liberatori和主唱Erika Savastani共同打造。整体风格延续意大利前卫摇滚传统，融合现代意大利流行元素，既有首张专辑田园诗般的怀旧气质，也借鉴了九十年代意大利新前卫的手法。曲目编排兼具旋律的亲和力与复杂的器乐段落，亮点包括借鉴Le Orme与Banco等前辈精髓的若干作品。然而评论指出专辑最后四分之一略显疲软，部分曲目依赖电影化的氛围铺陈来弥补结构上的不足。与用户偏好的实验、前卫（avant-garde）、自由爵士、电子等方向相比，这是一张较为传统的意大利前卫摇滚作品，创新性有限。

items.body: Review by alainPP — An evolving, melodic, synth-driven sound; the track evokes human degradation in the face of AI."Tears Of The Muse" kicks off as a dark, mid-tempo rock track featuring 80s-style keyboards?somewhere between rock, prog, and dark wave. A thunderous beat reminiscent of Genesis and Gabriel gives way to a sharp riff and vocals that trade lines with a vocoder. "EKO" features a hook redolent of Saga?think sugary new-millennium prog-metal with Martin stepping in for Damian. A dash of Arena, a touch of Lalu?it works perfectly for this groovy track with its driving bassline. "I Am The One" features piano accompanying Simon's metronomic drumming. It has a rich, proggy sound?like Toto?complemented by a heavy riff and a solo from Joop. There's a groovy, jazzy, Yes-style break leading into a warm choral finale. "Mayacama" is an instrumental that channels Toto and Saga?I can't help but hear the resemblance. A guitar groove underpins the melody, building into a progressive crescendo with the keyboards following suit. A piano break and a synth-led ballad section precede Joop showing off his dexterity. "Prince With The Swift Warning" features rolling pads and vocal harmonies that add complexity, navigating between rock, pop, and ballad styles. It includes a tense break with a sharp guitar solo, an infectious rhythm, and a second solo that is delicate, bluesy, and proggy."Learning To Fly" features airy vocals and echoes of Saga?or even Marillion. It's an accessible track that surprises with its evolution, while a dark organ keeps the listener on edge. The guitar solo is pure prog, leading into a riff where Martin shows off his impressive vocal range, backed by Simon. The finale soars as Joop and then Vivien drive the track to a spine-tingling climax. "A Drop Of Water" is an acoustic guitar interlude featuring a brilliant, ear-piercing arpeggio?a nod to Steve Howe of Yes. "Fhloston Paradise"?named after the station in *The Fifth Element*?blends hard-hitting rock and vocoder with the energetic, percussive groove characteristic of Joop, reminiscent of Iron Maiden. It features a Yes-style coda, confirming Vivien's admiration for the band. "Cordal Weaves" is a unique track with ethereal, searching notes and a stereo soundscape that creates a distinctly progressive atmosphere. It offers a funky, simmering moment: Martin rallies the energy, Joop lays into the rhythm, and Simon unleashes a barrage of drums. The finale features soaring vocals and a guitar full of melancholic longing. "Midnight Ink" serves as a piano-bar-style closer, driven by a poignant, whispered croon. Melancholic strings lend the track a solemn tone?the perfect way to wrap up the album.A melting pot of mainstream rock in the vein of Saga, Yes, and Toto, created above all for the sheer joy of it. It offers a softer take on prog metal and an intense jazz-prog vibe that feels like a journey in a time capsule.
items._cn_summary: Lalu乐队这张专辑呈现出明显的旋律化前卫金属风格，融合了八十年代合成器音色与新千年流行金属的甜腻感。编曲涉及大量传统前卫摇滚元素，引用了Genesis、Yes、Saga、Toto、Marillion等乐队的风格特征，并加入了爵士段落和声乐变奏。专辑以人声为主导，键盘与吉他交替担任独奏角色，结构上偏向叙事性长篇作品。然而整体创作思路偏向主流摇滚审美，虽有少量实验性元素如声码器与立体声场处理，但缺乏真正的前卫突破或电子实验成分。与用户偏好的实验音乐、学术爵士、电子声学等方向距离较远，本质上仍是一张注重旋律可听性的传统前卫金属唱片。
